Daphnia magna

Daphnia magna is a small freshwater crustacean, the largest of the European water fleas, that drifts in ponds and lakes. It is mostly transparent, reproduces mainly by clones, and is one of the most widely used animals in ecology, genetics and toxicity testing.

Females measure about 3 to 5 mm and males about 2 mm. The body is bean-shaped and enclosed in a transparent carapace, with one large dark compound eye at the front and two pairs of antennae; the large, branched second pair drives swimming. Males have longer first antennae and a hooked first leg used to clasp females.

It lives in standing fresh and brackish water, from temporary pools to lakes, tolerating salinity up to about 8 parts per thousand and preferring roughly 18 to 22 °C. It is native to the Nearctic and Palearctic regions, with records in western Europe, around the Black Sea and in coastal rock pools of the north-eastern United States.
It is a filter feeder. Hairs on its thoracic legs strain particles, generally smaller than 50 micrometres, from the water: algae, bacteria, detritus and fungal spores.

It swims in quick, jerky jumps driven by its large second antennae. In lakes it can perform a daily vertical migration, rising to the upper water at night to feed and sinking by day to avoid predators. It lives in dense groups with no social hierarchy.

It is a cyclic parthenogen: most of the time females produce diploid eggs that develop into female clones, with a brood of about 8 eggs on average, held in the brood pouch for 1 to 4 days. Under stress such as low food, extreme temperature or crowding, males appear and fertilised eggs are enclosed in a protective case called an ephippium, which can remain dormant for years. Young reach maturity in 6 to 10 days.

Daphnia are often keystone grazers in ponds and lakes, the main consumers of unicellular algae, and they link primary production to fish and invertebrate predators. D. magna is eaten by fish such as roach and perch and by insect larvae and backswimmers, and in some habitats it can be displaced by competing Daphnia species.

The Animal Diversity Web states that the species has not been evaluated by the IUCN and has no special protection status. It is easy to culture and widespread, and no specific threat was found in the sources consulted.

Domestic cat
Felis catus

The domestic cat is a small carnivorous mammal descended chiefly from Near Eastern wildcats. Its association with people began around early farming settlements, where rodents gathered near stored grain. Cats spread widely with human travel while retaining much of their ancestral hunting behaviour.

A compact, four-legged feline, it has a flexible spine, padded feet, sensitive whiskers and retractile claws. Coat length, colour, pattern, body size and tail shape vary widely among individuals and breeds; most cats nevertheless share a broadly similar, agile build.

Cats now occur worldwide, especially around settlements. They live in homes, farms, towns and suburbs, while unowned or free-roaming populations often remain near present or former human habitation. Shelter, food supplied by people and access to small prey influence where they settle.

Cats are obligate meat-eaters. They stalk and ambush small prey, commonly rodents and birds, and may also catch reptiles, insects or fish. A free-roaming cat can hunt even when people provide food, so hunting is not simply a response to hunger.

Hunting combines quiet approach, a sudden pounce and a bite; play rehearses parts of this sequence. Cats communicate through posture, sound, touch and scent marks. Though often solitary and territorial, they can form social groups where food and shelter are concentrated.

Females can cycle repeatedly during a breeding season, with timing affected by daylight and conditions. Mating commonly induces ovulation; pregnancy lasts roughly two months. Kittens are born dependent, nursed by their mother, and gradually weaned over their first weeks; paternal care is uncommon.

Free-ranging cats also kill native wildlife, and research documents predation across many regions and islands. The outcome varies with prey, habitat, cat density and human feeding; island species can be especially vulnerable.

The species is widespread through human care, but introduced, free-ranging populations create local conservation problems where native prey lack defences against mammalian hunters. Such impacts concern particular ecosystems and do not describe every domestic cat.

Dugong
Dugong dugon

The dugong is a fully marine sirenian and the only living member of Dugongidae. It ranges through tropical coastal waters from East Africa and the Red Sea across the Indian Ocean to the western Pacific, where seagrass grows. Unlike manatees, some of which enter rivers, the dugong has a notched tail fluke rather than a rounded paddle. Its life follows shallow seagrass beds: it feeds and rests nearby, and moves when food patches shift or deteriorate.

An adult has a heavy, tapered body, short foreflippers and no visible hind limbs. Its broad muzzle turns down toward the seabed; a flexible upper lip and sensory bristles help it find and pull plants. Sparse hair covers the grey skin, which can look brown or green where algae grow. The tail has two pointed lobes. Males may develop small tusks from their upper incisors. Together, the downturned muzzle and fluked tail distinguish the dugong from manatees and suit a slow-swimming grazer of the seabed. Adults are around three metres long and may weigh up to 500 kilograms.

Dugongs favour warm, shallow coastal waters with seagrass, especially protected bays, lagoons, channels and island shores. Most feeding occurs in shallow water, often less than 20 metres deep, though animals also use deeper meadows over broad, gently sloping shelves. Seagrass beds are patchy and vary in species, quality and seasonal growth. Tracking in Queensland and the Northern Territory found both relatively local animals and individuals travelling hundreds of kilometres. Movement is individual and food-linked; it is not one fixed migration route shared by all dugongs.

Seagrasses make up nearly all of the dugong’s diet. Its muzzle and bristled upper lip help it pull shoots from the sediment. Where plants can be uprooted, dugongs may eat leaves, rhizomes and roots; on firm ground or among resistant plants, they crop leaves instead. Root feeding is therefore conditional, not universal. At Ambon, Indonesia, field researchers recorded dugongs removing shoots and below-ground biomass from Halodule uninervis beds. Dugongs often select digestible, nutrient-rich species. Their trails through soft sediment show where grazing has disturbed the meadow.

Dugongs breathe air and surface between bouts of underwater feeding. They occur alone, in small groups or in larger feeding aggregations. Observations in Moreton Bay, Australia, found that animals in dense herds spent more time feeding, suggesting that food helped bring them together. Neighbours changed frequently, and the herds were not clearly organized as protection against predators. Mothers and calves remain close; calves sometimes travel or rest over their mothers’ backs. The same observations showed that mother–calf pairs spent more time near the surface than lone animals, increasing their exposure to boat strikes. These findings describe that bay rather than every dugong population.

Dugongs mature late and usually produce one calf after a pregnancy estimated at about fourteen months. Births are separated by several years, with longer intervals when food is poor, so populations replace lost adults slowly. The calf is born underwater. It nurses while also beginning to eat seagrass soon after birth. It remains close to her for roughly one or two years. Age at first birth and birth intervals vary among populations. In Torres Strait, reproduction was lower during a period of seagrass decline than when meadows were abundant, although food and population density could not be separated as causes.

As a large herbivore, the dugong changes the meadows where it feeds. Cropping leaves or excavating plants creates trails and alters the balance between shoots and underground parts. At one Indonesian site, grazing removed much of the shoots and upper below-ground biomass; tracks recovered during wet-season growth but not in the dry season. Effects are thus local and seasonal. Grazing produces a shifting pattern of cropped and intact patches, while seagrass meadows also shelter young fish and invertebrates. Dugong health and meadow condition are closely connected.

The amended global IUCN assessment of 2015, published in 2019, classifies the dugong as Vulnerable. Separate 2022 assessments classify the East African subpopulation as Critically Endangered and New Caledonia’s as Endangered. Those categories apply locally, not to the whole species. Fishing nets can entangle and drown dugongs; hunting, boat strikes, and seagrass loss or degradation add pressure. East Africa’s assessment reports very low numbers and fishing deaths. In New Caledonia, hunting and boat injuries combine with seagrass decline linked to coastal development, pollution and anchoring. Slow maturity and infrequent births impede recovery after adult losses.

Dunlin
Calidris alpina

The dunlin is a small wader and one of the most familiar shorebirds on coastal mudflats, where it gathers in flocks that can number in the thousands. Most of the dunlins seen in Britain in winter breed farther north and east.

An adult weighs about 50 g, with a wing near 119 mm. It has a long, slightly downcurved black bill and black legs. In summer the back is chestnut and the belly shows a black patch; in winter the plumage is a muted grey-brown above and white below. The sexes look alike, though females are slightly larger.

It breeds on grassland, moorland and Arctic tundra. In winter it is mainly coastal, especially on estuaries, bays and mudflats, and at high tide it roosts on nearby fields, saltmarsh and shorelines. A few birds use inland sites.

The dunlin eats mainly invertebrates: bivalves, worms, insect larvae, small crustaceans and snails. It feeds by sight and taste with a rapid pecking motion by day, and relies more on touch, probing the mud, at night.

Dunlins are highly social and form large flocks that twist and turn in tight formation. They are migratory: breeding birds from Britain mostly move south to Europe and North Africa, while the wintering birds come mainly from eastern Europe and Russia. Males defend nesting territories with aerial displays and trilling calls.

A pair typically raises one brood a year and lays four eggs (two to four). Both sexes incubate for 21–22 days. The downy chicks leave the nest quickly and fledge after about 19–21 days. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.

On the breeding grounds, nests are raided by weasels, Arctic foxes, jaegers and gulls; in winter, harriers, falcons and owls hunt dunlins exposed on mudflats. Because it depends on healthy estuaries, the species is considered an indicator of wetland condition.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern, but it has been Red-listed in the UK since 2021. About 350,000 dunlins winter in the UK, and the winter population fell by 22% between 1998 and 2023; milder Baltic winters may keep more birds farther east. The oldest ringed bird lived over 19 years.

Great Diving Beetle
Dytiscus marginalis

The great diving beetle is one of the largest beetles of Britain and Ireland and a fierce predator of still fresh water. It lives in the water as both larva and adult, yet it flies at night to colonise new ponds.

Adults are about 3 cm long, with a dark olive-brown, almond-shaped body flattened from top to bottom. The pronotum, the plate behind the head, is bordered all round with yellow, and the wing cases have a brownish-yellow edge. Females usually have ribbed wing cases while males have smooth ones, although some mainland European females are smooth.
It lives in still or very slow-flowing fresh water with plenty of submerged vegetation. It is native to the Palearctic, across Europe, Asia and northern Africa.
Adults and larvae are both predators. They eat other water insects, tadpoles and very small fish, hunting among submerged plants.

The adult comes to the surface from time to time and pushes out the tip of its abdomen to renew an air supply kept under its wing cases. It is a strong flier, mostly at night. When seized, it releases a foul-smelling fluid containing benzoic acid and related compounds.

Females lay eggs singly in submerged plant stems in early spring, and the eggs take about 18 days to hatch. The larvae grow quickly, reach about 5 cm, and by late summer leave the water to pupate in damp soil at the water’s edge. Young adults usually emerge in mid-autumn but stay buried through the winter.

Despite its soft body, the larva can tackle large prey such as young newts, froglets and small fish. The adult flies to colonise new ponds, and newly created garden ponds are often reached in their first year.

No global conservation assessment was found. In Britain the species is described as quite common and widespread, and the Animal Diversity Web lists no special protection status, while noting that European specialists are seeking protection beyond limits on collecting.

Straw-coloured Fruit Bat
Eidolon helvum
The straw-coloured fruit bat is one of the largest fruit bats of Africa and the most widespread. It roosts in very large colonies, makes long migrations and is listed as Near Threatened.

A large bat with a body of about 14–21 cm and a weight of 230–350 g, males being slightly bigger. The neck and back are straw-coloured and the underside a duller brown or grey. The wings are long and narrow, built for long flights, and the head is large and pointed with big eyes and no white facial markings. Wingspan is given as up to about 75 cm in one source and up to one metre in another.

It lives across most of sub-Saharan Africa and in the south-west of the Arabian Peninsula, in forest and savanna from coastal forest to dry regions, and from sea level to about 2,000 m. Tropical forest is its prime habitat because of the abundant food. It roosts mainly in tall trees and sometimes in caves, and also uses towns and farmland.

It sucks the juice from fruit and spits out the pulp. Reported foods include mangoes, dates, figs, pawpaws and avocados, as well as the flowers of baobab, Borassus palms and silk-cotton trees. It also chews soft wood and bark, apparently for moisture. It feeds in the open upper canopy and can eat a large quantity in a night.

It is social and nocturnal: colonies rest in trees by day and leave the roost at night in small groups, flying in straight lines and at greater heights than other fruit bats. It forages up to about 30 km from the roost and is noisy, chattering in the roost and while eating. It is a long-distance migrant: every year millions gather at Kasanka National Park in Zambia, and it holds the longest migration recorded for an African mammal.

It breeds once a year, with mating from April to June, and most populations show delayed implantation, so that births come in February and March. A single young of about 50 g is usual; it cannot fly at birth and only the female cares for it. The sources disagree on the total length of gestation (nine months or about 275 days).

By visiting flowers it pollinates trees of the mulberry and silk-cotton families, and by carrying fruit it disperses seeds. Owls, eagles, buzzards, snakes and civets prey on it, and it is eaten by people in parts of West and Central Africa. Where colonies roost near orchards it can be a crop pest.

It is listed as Near Threatened. Bushmeat hunting is a main cause of local declines in West and Central Africa, and deforestation is the greatest threat overall. In some areas bats are seen as pests and their roosts are destroyed. Reports of colony size vary widely, from tens of thousands to millions, and one source calls the species very abundant.

Emperor penguin
Aptenodytes forsteri

The emperor penguin is the largest living penguin, a flightless seabird that breeds through the Antarctic winter. Adults combine a large store of body fat with dense, layered feathers and heat-conserving circulation. When cold and wind intensify, birds gather in compact groups; this social thermoregulation complements their physical insulation and helps breeding males endure long fasts.

Adults stand about 115 centimetres tall and may weigh up to 40 kilograms at the start of breeding. Their mass changes substantially through fasting and breeding. The adult has a black head and back, a white breast and belly, and a broad pale-yellow patch along each side of the neck; juveniles have a duller patch. The similar king penguin is smaller, with a narrower, darker orange neck patch; in an emperor, the pale patch extends down to the waterline when it swims.

Breeding colonies lie around the Antarctic coast. Most occupy fast ice, frozen seawater attached to the continent; unlike many birds, emperors have no fixed nests and colonies can shift during winter storms. Nearby open-water polynyas give adults access to feeding areas even when sea ice is extensive; local ice conditions shape each colony’s position and timing.

At sea, emperor penguins pursue prey underwater, commonly diving 150–250 metres for three to six minutes, although much deeper and longer dives have been recorded. They eat fish, krill, other crustaceans and squid. In stomach samples from adults provisioning chicks at Amanda Bay in 1986, fish made up nearly all the measured diet, chiefly Antarctic silverfish. That result describes one colony and season: prey proportions vary among sites and years as local ocean conditions alter what is available. Adults can warm small, cold prey internally; breeding birds also return with stomach contents to feed their chicks.

Colonies are crowded but not defended as individual territories. During severe winter weather, males carrying eggs close ranks to conserve heat while continuing to incubate. At one observed colony, tightly packed huddles remained mostly still, then all birds took small coordinated steps every 30–60 seconds, passing a movement wave through the group. Courtship uses calls. Returning mates locate one another by voice in the noisy crowd.

The annual cycle begins as autumn sea ice thickens and adults return to colonies, usually around April. A pair lays one egg, which the female transfers to the male before leaving to feed at sea. The male balances the egg on his feet beneath a brood pouch. He incubates without feeding for 65–75 days, while his breeding-season fast, which begins before incubation, can last about four months. The female returns with food around hatching, and the parents exchange care and foraging shifts. If the chick hatches first, the fasting male can briefly feed it a secretion from his oesophagus. Newly hatched chicks weigh about 150–200 grams, have sparse down, and cannot yet regulate their temperature. At roughly 50 days they can thermoregulate and begin spending time in groups, or crèches, while adults forage. In early summer, down is replaced by waterproof juvenile feathers; young birds leave for the sea around December or January, with exact timing depending on development and ice.

Emperor penguins link midwater prey to larger Southern Ocean consumers. In spring samples from three western Ross Sea sites, Antarctic silverfish dominated fish prey and connected zooplankton to seabird predators. Their prey mix is not uniform: fish, crustaceans and squid contribute differently among regions, so penguin foraging reflects the local marine food web. At the Haswell Islands, a study found South Polar Skuas mainly scavenged frozen emperor penguin eggs and chicks; researchers judged their effect on emperor breeding success there negligible.

The IUCN assessment dated 26 February 2026 assigns category Endangered (A3bc). Its climate-dependent models estimate a 45% probability that the global population will decline by more than half by 2073; this is a projection, not a measured future count. On 9 April 2026, BirdLife International announced the move from Near Threatened to Endangered; its summary separately projects a halving by the 2080s. Satellite estimates indicated a loss of about 10% of the population between 2009 and 2018. Early breakup can remove the fast-ice platform before chicks have waterproof feathers. In 2022, researchers judged that four of five Bellingshausen Sea colonies probably suffered total breeding failure after exceptional sea-ice loss; colony abandonment was inferred from satellite images, not observed directly.

Emu
Dromaius novaehollandiae

The emu is Australia’s tallest native bird, a flightless runner living across much of the mainland. Rainfall shapes its movements and breeding opportunities. A distinctive feature of its life cycle is male-only incubation and care of striped, mobile chicks.

Adults stand 1.6–1.9 m, with shaggy grey-brown feathers, a sparsely feathered bluish head and neck, tiny wings and long legs. Each foot has three forward toes; ostriches are taller and have two. Chicks bear dark stripes.

Emus range across mainland Australia, from coastal regions and woodlands to open plains. They avoid rainforest and very arid areas. Where food or water varies, birds move in response to climate and rainfall, sometimes hundreds of kilometres.

They eat nutrient-rich fruits, seeds, flowers and young shoots, plus insects and small animals when available. Food changes seasonally with plant growth and rain; swallowed pebbles help the gizzard grind it. They generally avoid dry grass and mature leaves.

Usually seen alone, in pairs or loose groups, emus make low booming, drumming and grunting calls using a tracheal pouch. Strong legs support rapid running, zigzag escape from aerial predators and defensive kicks at close range.

Breeding often occurs in late autumn and winter, but varies regionally. The pair makes a shallow ground nest; after laying dark-green eggs, the female usually leaves. The male fasts while incubating for about eight weeks, then guards and accompanies striped chicks for months. They walk and forage soon after hatching.

On the NSW north coast, emus disperse native plant seeds over long distances; chicks also eat caterpillars and grasshoppers. Their movements between feeding and nesting sites require connected habitat. Roads, fences and land conversion can block travel or kill birds.

The species remains widespread on mainland Australia, but some local populations are declining. A 2020 NSW profile classifies the north-coast and Port Stephens population as endangered, citing habitat loss and fragmentation, altered fire, predators, traffic and barriers. This regional status does not establish a global category.

Eurasian Bittern
Botaurus stellaris
The Eurasian bittern is a secretive heron of dense reedbeds. It is far more often heard than seen: in spring the male’s deep, far-carrying boom announces his territory.

It is a stocky, mid-sized heron, about 64–80 cm long with a wingspan of 125–135 cm, weighing around 1.2 kg in Britain. The plumage is streaked brown, buff and black, which makes it strongly cryptic among reeds. Males are larger than females.

It lives in reedbeds, and breeding birds favour the largest and least disturbed ones. It does best in shallow water that deepens gradually beside deeper, sparsely vegetated water. On migration and in winter it also uses smaller, more open wetlands, but still prefers dense cover.
The bittern is a carnivore that eats mainly fish, amphibians, insects and aquatic crustaceans. It hunts in the shallow water of reedbeds.

It is highly secretive. When alarmed it stretches its neck and body upright so that its streaks line up with the reeds, and it may sway like reeds in the wind. It stalks prey slowly before striking, and the male’s boom, given in the breeding season, can carry for kilometres.

Males are polygynous and may mate with several females, which alone build the nest, incubate and rear the young. In Britain a clutch is typically four to six eggs, incubated for 25–26 days. The chicks are downy and fledge after about 50–55 days.

Nests are woven into vegetation over water, and the main causes of nest loss are predation and starvation of chicks. Predators such as the Eurasian mink and the raccoon dog are known to take its nests. Because its needs cover whole reedbed ecosystems, protecting the bittern benefits many other marsh species.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide, but in the UK it is Amber-listed, legally protected and scarce. Britain fell to a low of only 11 booming males in 1997, then recovered to 191 males in 2017. The oldest ringed bird reached nearly 12 years.

Eurasian Bullfinch
Pyrrhula pyrrhula
The Eurasian Bullfinch is a compact finch of wooded Europe and temperate Asia. Northern populations often move south in winter, while many remain resident.
Adults measure about 14.5–16 cm and show a stout black bill, grey back, black cap and wings, and white rump. Males have rose-red underparts; females are grey-brown, and juveniles lack the black cap.
It nests in mixed woodland, scrub and hedgerows, including wooded parks and gardens. Shrubs and leafy cover offer nest sites and sheltered feeding routes; it generally avoids open, treeless country.

Its short, powerful conical bill cracks seeds and clips buds from branches, often high in trees. Seeds and berries are important seasonally, while fruit-tree buds are especially taken in late winter and spring. A pouch at the floor of the mouth stores food, complementing the bill’s role in collecting it.
Pairs move quietly through cover, giving soft piping whistles that reveal birds hidden in foliage. Outside breeding, they usually travel as pairs or small family groups rather than large flocks.

The female builds a cup nest in a shrub or tree and usually lays four or five eggs, incubating them for 14–16 days. Downy chicks receive parental food, including small invertebrates, leave after about 15–17 days, and remain dependent while learning to forage. In Britain, breeding extends mainly from May to July, with nests of twigs, moss and lichen concealed in dense vegetation.

Sparrowhawks prey on adult bullfinches, while eggs and nestlings are vulnerable to other predators; dense nesting cover shelters these early stages. Their seasonal use of buds links them to woody plant growth and can bring them into conflict with orchard growers.

The global IUCN assessment published in 2018 classified the species as Least Concern because of its broad range. Regional declines can still occur: British monitoring records a long fall since the late 1970s, which may be affected by declining habitat quality and fewer large orchards.

Eurasian Hobby
Falco subbuteo
The Eurasian hobby is a small falcon and a superb aerial hunter. It chases dragonflies and even swallows through the air with fast, agile flight, and spends the winter in Africa.

About the size of a kestrel, 29–36 cm long with a wingspan of 74–84 cm; British adults weigh around 211 g. The upperparts are slate-grey, the underparts whitish with dark streaks, with white cheeks, a black moustache and rufous thighs and undertail. In flight the long, pointed wings look scythe-shaped, like a large swift. Juveniles are browner and lack the red.
It lives in open countryside such as lowland farmland, wetlands and heathland, often with scattered small woods. In Britain it was once mostly a bird of southern England but is spreading northwards.
It eats large flying insects such as dragonflies, and small birds, especially swallows and martins. It often eats small prey on the wing, passing it from its talons to its beak in flight.

The hobby hunts in fast, high-speed aerial chases and can accelerate quickly, and it often soars high. It is relatively secretive when breeding. It is a summer visitor to Britain, usually arriving from late April, with the last birds leaving in October.

A clutch is typically 2–3 eggs, incubated for about 28 days mainly by the female, and a single brood is raised. Chicks fledge after roughly 30–34 days. Eggs are laid between June and August, usually in an old nest built by crows. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.

As a predator of dragonflies and of hirundines, the hobby is tied to rich insect and bird populations over open country. It relies on nests built by other birds, such as crows, rather than building its own.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. The UK breeding population was estimated at 2,050 pairs in 2016; it is Green-listed and legally protected from disturbance at the nest. The oldest ringed bird recorded in Britain lived over 14 years.

Eurasian Jackdaw
Corvus monedula

The Eurasian Jackdaw, also classified as Coloeus monedula, is a small crow of Europe, western Asia and north-west Africa. Most populations are resident; northern and eastern birds move south in winter.

Adults measure 34–39 cm and weigh around 240 g. British ringing samples averaged 242 g for males and 226 g for females. Glossy black plumage, a grey nape and cheeks, short black bill and silvery-white eyes distinguish this crow. Young birds are browner with blue eyes.
It forages in open farmland and parks but nests in sheltered cavities: tree holes and rock clefts, or urban chimneys and towers.

This omnivore searches mostly on the ground, picking insects and other invertebrates from short vegetation and soil surfaces. During breeding, it takes surface and grass-dwelling prey from short turf and beneath dung; nestlings eat mainly insects and larvae. In winter, plant matter, especially grain and weed seeds, becomes more important. Fruit, carrion and refuse also supplement its diet. Jackdaws sometimes raid other birds’ nests for eggs or chicks.

Pairs feed and roost together, remaining close within noisy flocks. Their metallic “chack-chack” calls maintain contact, while a harsher call warns of danger. In experiments, jackdaws responded to human attention during competition for food and used a familiar person’s communicative cues to locate hidden food in a cooperative task.

Pairs often mate for life, breed from their second year and nest in colonies. They build a stick platform in a cavity, lining it with hair, wool or feathers. The female lays four or five pale blue-green eggs and incubates them for about 20 days as the male feeds her. Hatchlings are naked and helpless; both parents feed them. British nest records show fledging at about 32 days. Young then remain with their family for roughly another month while learning to feed independently.
Ground insects feed jackdaws, which also consume seeds and carrion. Cavity nests can be contested with other birds, and communal roosts concentrate large flocks.

Globally, the species is assessed as Least Concern; the broad European population trend has been stable. In Britain, breeding numbers rose from the 1960s to 2024. Historically, jackdaws were hunted for crop damage and nesting in belfries.

Eurasian jay
Garrulus glandarius

The Eurasian jay is a woodland corvid whose conspicuous blue wing patch contrasts with a life spent moving quietly through foliage. It forages both in trees and on the ground, shifting between seasonal food sources across its broad Eurasian range. Its reputation as an acorn carrier is well earned, but insects, fruits, seeds and animal prey also shape its diet and ecological effects.

In the European form, the body is warm pinkish brown, with a pale throat, black facial moustache and a crown of black-and-white streaked feathers that can be raised. The folded wing shows a vivid blue panel barred with black, beside white and black markings; in flight, the white rump flashes against the dark tail. In the British sample, adults averaged 167 grams; 90% of the 1,113 recorded weights fell between 144 and 189 grams. In northern Europe and France the nominate form has a pale, black-spotted crown, while British island forms are darker russet.

The species ranges from western Europe and North Africa east through much of temperate Asia, with local forms differing across this enormous span. It occupies mature deciduous, mixed and conifer woods, as well as parks and wooded farmland with cover.

This omnivore takes insects and other invertebrates, especially during the breeding season, as well as acorns, beech nuts, seeds, berries and cultivated fruit. It searches foliage and branches for caterpillars and beetle larvae, probes leaf litter and soil, and takes eggs or nestlings when opportunities arise. A strong bill helps open hard foods, while its seasonal variety reduces dependence on any single crop and supplies protein to growing chicks.

A rough, rasping screech often gives away a bird hidden in the canopy; calls can alert nearby animals, and playback experiments found that red squirrels increased vigilance or fled after hearing jay alarms. In autumn, jays carry acorns away from oak crowns and bury them singly or in small caches, then retrieve many later. In a laboratory food-hiding task, seven jays that watched an experimenter hide mealworms under cups later used incidental visual details of that event in an unexpected test after a delay.

Pairs usually produce one brood a year, laying commonly four or five eggs in a well-concealed nest of twigs in a tree or shrub. Both sexes incubate for about 18 days, and the naked, helpless nestlings typically remain in the nest for roughly 21 days before fledging. Parents continue feeding young after they leave, while breeding timing and success vary with food and local conditions.

By carrying viable acorns and burying them away from parent trees, jays provide seed dispersal: some unrecovered seeds can germinate in suitable conditions and establish new oaks. In a four-country Central European field study, jays foraged on oak trees whose acorns were narrower than those on the nearest unused trees. Nest cameras in Britain and Ireland also recorded jays taking songbird broods, showing how seed dispersal coexists with predation on other birds. A diet study in southern Finland recorded Eurasian jays among the prey of northern goshawks.

The global IUCN Red List assessment published in 2025 classifies the Eurasian jay as Least Concern. The 2021 European Red List classifies it as Least Concern with a stable EU population trend. European monitoring reported a moderate increase; in France, counts rose 23 percent between 2001 and 2019. These broad indicators do not describe every local population.

Eurasian nuthatch
Sitta europaea
Across temperate Eurasia, the mostly resident Eurasian nuthatch depends on mature trees for bark rich in food and cavities for nests.

Adults are 12–14.5 cm long and weigh about 19–26 g. The compact body, short tail, pointed bill, blue-grey back and black eye stripe are distinctive; European birds often have buff underparts, while northern forms are paler. Males have darker chestnut flanks than females.

It favours mature deciduous or mixed woodland, especially old trees with holes. Parks and orchards also suit it when such trees remain; most populations stay year-round, while juveniles disperse and some northern birds move after poor cone crops.

In spring and summer it gleans caterpillars, beetles, spiders and other small invertebrates from bark, crevices and buds; nestlings receive mainly insects. Seeds and nuts matter more in autumn and winter. The bird wedges hard food into a bark crack to hammer it open, and caches surplus seeds for later.
Curved claws grip bark, allowing headfirst descent. Pairs hold territories year-round. The species is highly vocal, with repeated loud whistles and sharper alarm calls.

The pair nests in a tree cavity, often an old woodpecker hole. A nuthatch narrows an oversized entrance with dried mud, leaving a small opening that limits access for larger competitors. The female usually lays six to eight eggs and incubates them for about 16–17 days. Young fledge at about 24 days and remain dependent for roughly one to two weeks.
By using old woodpecker holes, the nuthatch depends on cavity-building birds as well as ageing trees. Larger competitors, such as starlings, are excluded by the mud-narrowed entrance.

The species is widespread; the IUCN assessment published in 2018 classified it as Least Concern, with a stable global population. Loss and fragmentation of old woodland can still remove nest cavities and feeding surfaces, causing local declines. In Britain, monitoring records a strong increase from 1967 to 2024.

Eurasian Oystercatcher
Haematopus ostralegus

The Eurasian oystercatcher is a large, stocky black-and-white wader that is a familiar sight on shores and estuaries. It is also an adaptable bird: over the last fifty years some have begun to breed inland, even on urban rooftops.

The plumage is black and white, with a long orange-red bill and pinkish-red legs. In flight it shows a broad white wing stripe, a black tail and a white rump that extends in a V between the wings. British adults average about 546 g (465–640 g) and have a wing length of 251–275 mm.

In Britain breeding birds are most frequent on estuaries and also common on open shore, but many nest inland, especially in northern Britain, along rivers and in wet meadows. In winter it occupies rocky and estuarine shores, with the largest concentrations on major estuaries.
It eats cockles and mussels, which it prises open or hammers open with its strong bill. In winter on The Wash, birds rely heavily on cockles and blue mussels.

From autumn, oystercatchers gather in large flocks along the shore, and on the British east coast resident birds are joined by others from Norway. Morecambe Bay holds the most wintering birds in the UK, about 40,000 counted at high-tide roosts in a recent winter. Ringing shows little exchange between the Atlantic and continental populations.

In Britain the average first clutch date is 19 May. The typical clutch is two or three eggs, incubated by both sexes for 24–27 days. The chicks are downy and active from hatching and fledge after 34–37 days. There is one brood a year, and breeding typically starts at age four.

Because it eats cockles, the oystercatcher is vulnerable where cockle beds are overfished. In the Netherlands, shellfisheries have been linked to lower winter survival. Inland, a 95% decline between 1990 and 2015 at one Perthshire study site was attributed to land-use change.

The IUCN lists it as Near Threatened globally, and it is Amber-listed in the UK. The UK breeding population was 96,000 pairs in 2016 and fell by 23% between 1995 and 2024; the main causes of the recent decline are unclear. A bird that reaches breeding age lives about 12 years; the oldest ringed bird passed 41.

Eurasian Sparrowhawk
Accipiter nisus
The Eurasian sparrowhawk is one of the smallest diurnal birds of prey in Europe. It is a secretive hunter of small birds, and the female is much larger than the male.

In Britain a male weighs about 150 g and has a wing near 198 mm, while a female weighs about 266 g with a wing near 234 mm. The male has a blue-grey back and fine reddish barring below; the female is brown or grey-brown above with brown barring. Both have short, rounded wings, a long tail, long legs and a sharply hooked bill.
In Britain the sparrowhawk breeds mostly in deciduous and coniferous woodland, and it prefers varied woodland. In lowland England it also uses hedges as cover for hunting.

It feeds mainly on small birds, which can make up most of its diet, especially ground-feeding species such as finches, thrushes and warblers. It occasionally takes small mammals. Males take lighter prey than the larger females, and birds are often plucked at a regular post.

The sparrowhawk is solitary and territorial. It hunts by dashing out from cover or from a hidden perch to chase prey low and fast, and its flight alternates flapping with short glides. It also visits garden bird feeders in search of prey.

In Britain a typical clutch is four or five eggs, incubated by the female for about 33 days. The chicks fledge at around 28 days, and birds usually first breed at one year old. The male courts with aerial displays and does most of the early hunting for the family.

As a predator of small birds and mammals, the sparrowhawk helps regulate their numbers. Adults have few natural enemies, though the northern goshawk sometimes raids nests. The species also carries blood parasites such as avian malaria.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide, and in the UK it is Amber-listed. The UK breeding population was estimated at about 31,000 pairs in 2016. The oldest ringed bird reached 17 years.

Eurasian Teal
Anas crecca

The Eurasian teal is a small, fast dabbling duck of marshes and estuaries. In Britain it is much more numerous in winter, when about half a million birds arrive from the Continent, than in the breeding season.

In Britain, males average about 336 g with a wing of 190 mm; females are smaller, around 303 g and 182 mm. The male has a chestnut head with a broad green eye patch, a spotted chest, grey flanks and a black-edged yellow patch under the tail. The female is mottled brown. Both sexes show a bright green wing patch.

In winter it uses low-lying wetlands in the south and west, from small pools to large estuaries, on coast and fresh water. In the breeding season it is thinly and patchily distributed, with a preference for northern moors and mires and some sites in southern Britain and Ireland.

The teal is an opportunistic feeder, taking insects and their larvae, seeds and aquatic plants. It skims food from the surface or filters it through the comb-like plates of its bill. Ducklings eat mostly insect larvae at first.

Winter flocks are made up largely of birds from around the Baltic and Siberia. Numbers in Britain peak between October and February, and the species is scarce in summer. Teal gather in large groups, which helps them find food and spot danger, and they rarely dive except to escape predators.

In Britain a pair typically raises one brood a year. The female lays 8–11 eggs and incubates them alone for 21–23 days; the ducklings leave the nest soon after hatching and fledge at about 25–30 days. Teal can breed from one year of age.

Teal carry seeds in their droppings and feed alongside other dabbling ducks, sharing vigilance. Eagles, harriers and falcons hunt loafing birds, foxes take incubating females, and crows and other nest raiders eat eggs. The UK supports a significant share of the north-west European wintering population.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern, but it is Amber-listed in the UK. About 2,700 pairs bred there in 2016, and about 435,000 birds wintered in 2012–17; the winter population rose by 14% between 1998 and 2023, though the breeding range has shrunk by 16.5% since 1968–72. The oldest ringed bird lived over 18 years.

European green crab
Carcinus maenas

The European green crab is a common shore crab native to the north-east Atlantic and nearby European and North African coasts. Human transport has also established it on distant shores, where it can become invasive.

Its broad carapace may reach about 9 cm across, with records near 10 cm outside its native range. Five teeth sit behind each eye and three lobes between them; C. aestuarii, its Mediterranean relative, has a smoother, projecting front. The first of its five pairs of legs bears claws; the other four are walking legs. Colour varies from green to orange or red.

It inhabits sheltered shores, estuaries and shallow subtidal waters, on mud, sand, rock or submerged vegetation. Its tolerance of changing salinity helps it live across tidal creeks and estuarine margins.
It is an omnivore, eating mussels, clams, worms, small crustaceans, algae and carrion. Its claws handle or crush prey, while smaller mouthparts move food to the mouth.

Growth requires moulting: the crab sheds its rigid exoskeleton, expands beneath a soft replacement, which then hardens. Female urine carries sex pheromones that attract males before mating. Feeding often peaks at night around high tide.

Males guard females before mating, which follows the female’s moult while her new shell is soft. The male transfers spermatophores, or sperm packets; the female can store sperm and later attach fertilized eggs beneath her abdomen. Eggs hatch into planktonic zoeae, pass through four stages, then become megalopae, crab-shaped larvae that settle and moult into bottom-living juveniles. In a North American monitoring report, the zoea phase lasted 17–80 days and the megalopa 5.5–26 days, with temperature affecting timing.

Eelgrass beds provide nursery habitat for juvenile fish and invertebrates, so crab damage can reduce this shelter. Adults can uproot shoots while digging for prey, and juveniles may graze the soft tissue at their bases. Waves and currents can dislodge shoots whose roots have been weakened.

Introduced populations can threaten shellfish and coastal habitats through predation and disturbance. Monitoring in introduced regions aims to limit further spread and protect local shellfish and habitats.

European Herring Gull
Larus argentatus

The herring gull is the classic large seaside gull of Europe. Originally a cliff-nesting coastal bird, it has adapted to towns and cities, nesting on rooftops, but its numbers in Britain have fallen sharply.

A large gull of 54–60 cm. In Britain, adults average about 970 g with a wing of 415 mm. Adults have a pale grey back, white underparts, black wingtips with white spots, pink legs and a heavy yellow bill with a red spot. First-year birds are mottled brown.

Breeding birds are most frequent on open shores and cliffs, but some nest on buildings in towns. Outside the breeding season it is widespread across lowland Britain, mostly near the coast, and inland around rubbish tips, fields, reservoirs and lakes.

It feeds mainly on marine animals, the green shore crab being a particular favourite, and also on fish, insects, carrion and refuse. It is an opportunist; it even stamps its feet to imitate rain and bring earthworms to the surface.

Herring gulls forage in large flocks at refuse sites and are highly defensive of their nests and young. Pairs are often lifelong partners and return to the same nest site each year. In towns, rooftop nesting gives them plenty of food and fewer predators.

A pair raises one brood a year, laying typically three eggs (two to four), usually from mid-April, on the ground, on cliff ledges or on rooftops. The female does most of the 28–30 days of incubation. The chicks fledge at 35–40 days and peck the red spot on a parent’s bill to beg for food. Breeding typically starts at four years of age.

As a scavenger and predator of shore animals the herring gull exploits both natural and human food sources. Tracking of breeding birds at one colony showed most feeding on mussel beds and intertidal areas, while declining marine food is thought to push birds to forage inland.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern, but it is Red-listed in the UK. About 130,000 pairs bred there in 1998–2002 and some 740,000 birds wintered in 2003–06; the coastal breeding population fell by more than 50% between 1969–70 and 1998–2002 and appears to have kept falling. In ringing data the oldest birds reach about 12 years.

European lobster
Homarus gammarus
The European lobster is a clawed marine crustacean native to the northeastern Atlantic, Mediterranean and western Black Sea.

Its blue, mottled upper shell contrasts with a pale yellowish underside, long antennae and a segmented abdomen. Pot-caught animals commonly measure about 23–38 centimetres, rather than the much larger sizes reported for exceptional specimens. The ten walking limbs include a massive crushing claw and a sharper cutting claw, which perform complementary feeding functions. Growth requires shedding the rigid shell and expanding before the new shell hardens: this is moulting. Heating breaks the protein complex holding the red pigment astaxanthin, explaining the colour change from blue to red during cooking.

It occupies rocky seabeds from the lower shore to around 60 metres, sheltering in crevices, holes and excavated tunnels. The short, spiny projection at the front of the head is the rostrum, another useful identification feature.

Adults eat crabs, molluscs, sea urchins, marine worms and other bottom-living animals, sometimes taking fish or algae. Feeding declines in winter as colder water slows metabolism, so food intake changes with seasonal conditions.
Usually solitary and territorial, it hides during the day and emerges mainly at night to search for food. A rapid contraction of the abdomen and tail can propel it backwards when escape is needed.

Mating generally joins a hard-shelled male with a recently moulted, soft-shelled female, which can store his sperm before laying. Fertilized eggs remain attached beneath her abdomen for roughly nine to twelve months, with development influenced by water temperature. She fans water over the eggs to maintain oxygenation; hatchlings then enter the plankton, drifting near the sea surface. Successive moults produce the first juvenile stage, which resembles a miniature lobster and settles into sand or gravel rather than remaining in surface waters.

The planktonic phase exposes larvae to many predators; after settlement, buried juveniles gain protection from seabed shelter. Newly moulted lobsters are particularly vulnerable until their replacement shell hardens, making access to shelter essential.

Its global status is Least Concern, although commercial fishing creates substantial pressure in parts of its range; lobster pots are the main capture method. In Cornwall, hatchery programmes rear young through their vulnerable planktonic phase before releasing juveniles to coastal seabeds.

European Nightjar
Caprimulgus europaeus

The European nightjar is a secretive, nocturnal summer visitor to Europe, far more often heard than seen. Its mechanical, churring song carries across heaths at dusk, and old folklore claimed it drank goats’ milk, hence the name “goatsucker”.

The bird is 26–28 cm long, slightly smaller than a kestrel, with grey-brown plumage mottled, streaked and barred like bark. It has pointed wings, a long tail, large dark eyes and a small, very wide mouth. Males show white patches on the throat and near the wing and tail tips. British adults weigh 63–88 g, females being heavier.

In Britain it breeds on lowland heathland and on recently felled or newly planted conifer plantations, and more locally on moorland, woodland clearings and coastal dunes. Tracking shows that it also feeds over grassland and other non-forest habitats.
It hunts flying insects, especially moths, at dusk and dawn. GPS tracking in Britain showed fast foraging flights, sometimes over 3 km, to feeding sites that the birds revisit on later nights.

By day it relies on stillness and camouflage and at night it flies almost silently. The male sings a rising and falling churr, often turning his head and adding wing claps. It reaches Britain in late April or May and leaves in late August or September to winter south of the equatorial forest, especially in the south of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The eggs are laid on bare ground. The typical clutch is two eggs, incubated by both sexes for about 18 days, and the downy chicks fledge after roughly 18 days. In Britain the average first clutch date is 23 June, and a pair typically raises one or two broods. Breeding usually starts at one year old.

As a predator of night-flying insects, the nightjar helps limit their numbers. Its eggs on the ground are taken by foxes, hedgehogs and corvids, and adults can fall prey to owls and diurnal raptors, so camouflage is its main defence. Habitat loss is its main pressure.

The IUCN global category is Least Concern. In Britain it is Amber-listed, with about 4,600 males in 2004, after a decline of 51% between 1972 and 1992 followed by a recovery. The main threats are the loss of heathland and afforestation. A bird that reaches breeding age lives about four years; the oldest ringed bird was over 12.

European polecat
Mustela putorius

The European polecat is a wild mustelid that ranges across much of Europe and western Eurasia, where it hunts small vertebrates. The domestic ferret is a domesticated form of the polecat, and the two can interbreed to produce fertile hybrids. Their fur and facial markings overlap enough that field identification may be uncertain, and genetic testing may be needed to distinguish hybrids from wild polecats.

Its long, low body has short legs and a comparatively short, bushy tail. Dark guard hairs over a pale yellowish underfur create a grizzled coat; the pale muzzle, eyebrows and ear margins frame a dark facial mask. Adult British males are about 33–45 cm long and 0.8–1.9 kg, while females are 32–39 cm and 0.5–1.1 kg; the tail adds 12–19 cm.

The polecat occupies a broad range of landscapes, but in France it is especially associated with wetlands and river margins. British polecats often use hedged farmland and small woods, resting in rabbit burrows, hay bales or farm outbuildings as prey and shelter shift seasonally.

It is a carnivore whose prey changes with place and season: rabbits and other small mammals are important, with frogs, birds and other animals also taken. In a British stomach-content study of animals collected in 2012–2016, lagomorph remains occurred most often, followed by other mammals, amphibians and birds. Rabbits were more frequent in spring and summer than in autumn in that sample, illustrating how prey availability shapes a local diet. Its slender body lets it hunt rabbits inside their burrows.

The polecat is solitary; during breeding, males may mate with several females. Its movements are mainly nocturnal or crepuscular, although it can also be active by day. Radio-tracking there found that time spent foraging and travelling varied with food categories, while mating and breeding also changed activity. In that sample, activity averaged about seven and a half hours daily; females spent more time foraging, while males travelled more. Anal scent glands release a pungent secretion under stress and may also help communicate with neighbours, possibly limiting direct aggression.

In France, mating usually occurs in March–April; births follow in May–June after 40–42 days of gestation, without delayed implantation. One annual litter is usual, with one to twelve kits and weaning at about six weeks. Born blind and helpless, kits stay with their mother, become independent at three months and reach sexual maturity at ten to eleven months.

As a predator, the polecat takes rabbits, amphibians and birds, linking terrestrial and wetland food webs. In western France, tracking found marshy habitats associated with greater male mating success, while pregnant or nursing females shifted towards deciduous woodland.

The global IUCN assessment published in 2016 classified the species as Least Concern while noting that population trends were uncertain across much of its range. A French survey in 2017 found sparse, fragmented populations in many regions, with evidence varying greatly among areas. Documented pressures include habitat loss and fragmentation, trapping, road deaths, pollution and disease. In Britain, persecution and fur hunting severely reduced the polecat’s range before the population recovered.

Barton Springs Salamander
Eurycea sosorum

The Barton Springs salamander is a small, fully aquatic salamander of the springs of Austin, Texas. It keeps its larval, gill-breathing form for its whole life and never leaves the water, depending entirely on groundwater from the Edwards Aquifer.

Adults measure about 6–8 cm in total length. The head is broad and deep, with reduced eyes and three bright red, feathery gills on each side. The limbs are long and slender, and the short tail has a well-developed upper fin. The mottled upper body ranges from brown to purple, reddish or orange, and the underside is cream and often translucent. Its relative the Austin blind salamander has skin-covered eyespots.

It lives in clean water fed by the Edwards Aquifer, usually in the wet upper layer of gravel and rock in or near spring openings, pools and spring runs. The water stays near 20 °C all year. It first became known from four spring sites in Zilker Park, and has since been found at 12 more spring and cave sites in Hays and Travis Counties.

It is an opportunistic predator of small live invertebrates and prefers planarian flatworms. When these become scarce it switches to midge larvae and the amphipod Hyalella azteca, which an earlier account gave as its main food.

It spends much of its time in the spaces among stones and gravel of the streambed, which give it food, shelter from predators and refuge in drought. It is secretive and appears to be nocturnal, and it can tell low-risk predators from high-risk ones.

Females with eggs and young larvae are found all year, suggesting breeding in every season. Courtship includes a tail-straddling walk; the male leaves a sperm packet that the female picks up, and fertilisation is internal. Eggs have rarely been found in the wild. In captivity they hatch 15–40 days after laying, and the larvae begin to feed about 10–11 days later.

It feeds on small invertebrates of the spring’s stream bed, and its own predators are thought to include small fishes and crayfish. Its survival is tied to the quality and quantity of groundwater from the Edwards Aquifer.

It was listed as Endangered under the US Endangered Species Act on 30 April 1997, mainly because urban growth was reducing the quality and quantity of water feeding the springs. Its small range leaves it exposed to groundwater contamination, hazardous spills and increased water withdrawals. Its range is larger than first thought, but no population counts are given in the federal profile.

Fire salamander
Salamandra salamandra

The fire salamander is a robust, long-tailed amphibian of Europe whose life joins damp woodland with freshwater nurseries. Most adults live on land, while their offspring begin life as gilled larvae in streams or pools. This split means a healthy population needs both sheltered ground and suitable water within reach. Its conspicuous pattern and secretive habits make it easier to recognize than to observe.

An adult has a broad head, stout trunk, four short limbs and a rounded tail; in Central Europe adults commonly measure about 14-17 cm from snout to tail tip, with larger individuals reaching around 20-23 cm. Females tend to be heavier and slightly larger, especially when carrying embryos. The smooth, glossy black back bears irregular yellow spots or bands, sometimes orange or reddish; each pattern is distinctive, but its exact form varies among individuals and regions. Skin glands release secretions containing toxic alkaloids, including samandarine and samandarone. These chemicals can deter predators, but do not prevent every attack.

Across much of its range, the species favours deciduous and mixed woodland with cool, moist soil, leaf litter and hiding places such as dead wood, rock gaps and root hollows. Adults shelter by day and may roam through the forest floor at night, so a stream alone cannot provide the habitat they need. Females use springs, headwater streams and sometimes ponds or other still waters to release larvae; local choice depends on what water bodies are available. Forest cover, clean water and connected refuges together make a usable landscape.
On land, adults hunt small invertebrates such as earthworms, woodlice, beetles and slugs, swallowing each prey whole. Aquatic larvae hunt small water-dwelling animals, especially insect larvae.

The salamander is mainly nocturnal and becomes easier to see on rainy nights, when its skin is less exposed to drying. Adults breathe air with lungs, while aquatic larvae use external gills; in dry weather adults seek cool crevices, burrows or shelter beneath logs. During courtship, males may compete or interfere with rivals near a female.

Mating takes place on land: the male courts the female at close range and deposits a gelatinous spermatophore on the ground, which she takes up with her cloaca. Sperm is stored inside her, so fertilisation is internal; after gestation, she usually enters shallow water and releases fully formed, gilled larvae rather than laying eggs there. Many populations give birth to several dozen larvae, but two localized Iberian lineages independently evolved births of near-metamorphosed or fully terrestrial juveniles. In Central Europe larvae commonly metamorphose in roughly 40–120 days, losing their gills as lungs and limbs support life on land; timing changes with water conditions and food.

In pond-breeding populations, larvae prey on aquatic invertebrates and can affect local food webs. In a studied pond-adapted Central European population, females brought nutrients from land into ponds with their broods, and metamorphs carried some biomass back onto land; the return was smaller than the initial input because many larvae died and survivors were small. Larvae and adults are themselves food for other predators, although an adult’s glandular secretion can make it an unpalatable meal.

The global IUCN Red List classifies Salamandra salamandra as Vulnerable; the assessment was made on 26 July 2022 and published in 2023, so its category is not a current count at every site. Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans, or Bsal, is a chytrid fungus that infects skin and has been linked to severe, documented population declines in the Netherlands and Belgium. At Het Bunderbos in the Netherlands, one population fell by about 99.9% within seven years of the suspected introduction. EFSA notes that the historical route into Europe is not established and that a causal link between Bsal and declines in wild populations is not always clear; amphibian trade is a suspected pathway. Habitat loss, road deaths and drained springs threaten some populations.

Large flying fox
Pteropus vampyrus

The large flying fox is a fruit-eating bat of tropical Southeast Asia and one of the world’s largest bats. Its fox-like face, pointed ears and broad wings distinguish it from small insect-eating bats. It roosts by day in trees and leaves after dusk to feed, sometimes crossing national borders between feeding areas and roosts.

Adults have a forearm about 180–220 mm long, a wingspan commonly reported near 1.5 m, and a mass of roughly 0.6–1.1 kg. A dark mantle covers the head and shoulders; its tones range from reddish mahogany to nearly black, while the underside is also often dark. The long fingers support a thin wing membrane, and clawed thumbs and hind feet help the bat cling to branches. Fur colour varies with age and sex.

The species uses lowland tropical forest, mangroves, swamps, river margins, islands and, in some places, orchards and cultivated landscapes. Day roosts are often in tall trees, including mangroves and coconut groves. In a Malaysian field study, roosts were occupied seasonally as well as continuously, so a temporarily empty tree site did not by itself show that the colony had disappeared.

Fruit is the principal food, supplemented by flowers, nectar and pollen. The bat can use its teeth to open fruit and its long tongue to take soft pulp or liquid nectar. It searches for food at night with vision and smell; unlike echolocating insect hunters, it relies on sight rather than laryngeal echolocation for flight navigation. Local food choices vary with what is fruiting or flowering.

Large flying foxes gather in conspicuous tree roosts, where individuals hang head-down and may spread or wrap their wings around the body. Colonies can shift between roosts, and counts fluctuate over time. Satellite tracking in Peninsular Malaysia documented long nocturnal feeding flights and movements between Malaysia, Sumatra and Thailand. These observations came from a small, male-biased sample, so they do not describe every animal’s routine. Field and captive studies also describe a social hierarchy; colonies may contain smaller harems centred on one male, although that grouping should not be assumed at every roost.

Females generally produce one pup in an annual breeding cycle, although timing differs by region. Reports place births in March or early April in Thailand and in April–May in the Philippines; these dates should not be treated as universal. A newborn is furred and open-eyed but still depends on its mother. She carries it during the first days, then leaves it at the roost while foraging; nursing continues for about two to three months.

A field diet study at Subic Bay examined droppings of the Philippine subspecies P. vampyrus lanensis: Ficus seeds occurred in 66% of its samples, and Ficus variegata seeds in 34%. This shows that seeds pass through this bat’s gut, although it does not by itself prove successful seedling establishment. Fruit and flower feeding can move plant material, but the species-specific effects on pollination and forest regeneration remain incompletely measured.

Hunting and loss or degradation of roosting and feeding habitat threaten populations. A 2003–2006 Peninsular Malaysian study counted at least 21,600 bats across surveyed roosts and estimated licensed hunting at about 22,000 per year in 2002–2005; its population models suggested that this level could be unsustainable. Those are historical, regional findings, not current range-wide counts. The global IUCN Red List category changed from Near Threatened to Endangered in the 2022 update. In the separate Peninsular Malaysia Mammal Red List of 2017, it was categorized regionally as Endangered.

Common Snipe
Gallinago gallinago

The common snipe is a skulking, long-billed wading bird of wet ground, so well camouflaged that it is usually seen only when it bursts into a zigzag flight. In spring the male produces a strange drumming sound in display flight.

An adult weighs about 108 g with a wing length near 14 cm, and a length of roughly 23–28 cm. The plumage is mottled brown above with pale buff stripes along the back, a streaked breast and pale underparts. The bill is long and straight, about 6 cm, and the legs are short. The sexes look alike.

In the breeding season in Britain it is most frequent around lakes and also common in bogs and marshes, with the highest densities in Scotland, north-west England, Wales and western Ireland. In winter it uses a wide range of lowland and upland wet habitats. It nests on drier grassy ground close to its feeding areas.

It probes wet soil with its long bill for invertebrates. From April to August earthworms and insect larvae make up most of its food; in a Northumberland study, earthworms were about 61% of the diet by dry mass, followed by crane fly larvae at about 24%. Plant matter and seeds are eaten in smaller amounts.

A skulking bird, it keeps to cover and flushes with a jinking flight. In display the male dives so that air passes through his outer tail feathers, making the drumming sound; females seem to prefer males that drum well. Males and females also take part in display fights.

In Britain the first clutch is laid on average around 30 April, typically four eggs, with one brood. The female incubates alone for 18–20 days. The downy chicks leave the nest and fledge after about 19–20 days, tended by both parents. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.

As a predator of earthworms and larvae, the snipe is part of wet-grassland food webs, and it falls prey to red foxes, carrion crows and stoats. It is also hunted for food and sport, an estimated 1.5 million birds a year in Europe. In Britain, steep declines have been noted in lowland wet grassland.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide, but numbers have declined across Europe since 1980. In the UK it is Amber-listed: about 67,000 breeding pairs in 2016, with a breeding range 31.5% smaller than in 1968–72. A snipe typically lives about three years once adult, and the oldest ringed bird exceeded 16.

Giant panda
Ailuropoda melanoleuca

The giant panda is a bear of central China, now confined to scattered mountain forests in Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu. Its diet is almost entirely bamboo, although its body remains recognizably that of a bear rather than a specialized grazing mammal. Adults usually forage alone, but overlapping ranges and scent trails help them find one another during the breeding season.

The panda has a broad head, sturdy body and dense woolly coat: black fur marks its ears, eye patches, shoulders and legs, while its face and trunk are white. Adults are about 1.2 to 1.8 metres long; wild males can reach 113 kilograms and females rarely reach 104 kilograms, figures near the upper end rather than typical weights. Strong jaw muscles and broad molars crush tough bamboo stems. Beside five ordinary digits, each forepaw has an enlarged radial sesamoid, a small wrist bone covered by a fleshy pad. This so-called pseudo-thumb is relatively immobile: the five fingers flex around a bamboo stalk against it, while the panda’s teeth tear the stalk. The bone acts as a passive stop, not an active pinching finger, and its form balances feeding grip with bearing weight when the paw meets the ground.

Wild pandas survive in six mountain systems across Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu, in moist broadleaf or conifer forests with bamboo beneath the canopy. These forests usually lie around 1,500 to 3,000 metres above sea level, often under heavy rain or mist. In one Foping study in the Qinling Mountains, six GPS-collared pandas shifted between lower and higher ranges as different bamboo shoots and leaves came into season. That local pattern shows how a home range can include several feeding zones rather than one bamboo patch. Farming, timber extraction and forest clearing have removed lowland habitat, while broken forest can obstruct travel and contact between populations.

Bamboo is the panda’s staple food, and a wild adult may spend about 12 hours a day feeding. Across the year it selects tender shoots, leaves and stems as their availability changes. Its short digestive tract resembles that of other bears and extracts little energy from bamboo; it ferments plant fibre only to a limited degree. Captive feeding trials found low energy digestibility on bamboo-only diets, so much of the food’s energy remains unavailable to the animal. Field estimates put daily intake at roughly 13 to 15 kilograms of leaves and stems, while intake of watery shoots can be much higher. A study of eight pandas—five captive and three wild—measured daily energy expenditure at 37.7 percent of the amount predicted for a mammal of similar size, consistent with a low-activity lifestyle that reduces energy needs.

Pandas are mostly solitary, yet overlapping ranges, scent stations and occasional meetings create a loose social network. Glands near the anus leave chemical marks on trees, rocks and paths; these can carry information about sex, individual identity and reproductive condition. During the short breeding season, pandas also call as they approach through dense bamboo. In playback trials, females distinguished individual males’ bleats, evidence that calls can help coordinate close encounters. At other times, scent marks often help animals avoid one another. Feeding alternates with rests of several hours; pandas also climb and swim, though most of their active time is spent on the ground.

Females come into heat once each spring, often for only two or three days, so mating is concentrated in a brief window. After fertilization, the embryo can pause before attaching to the uterus, a process called delayed implantation that shifts the timing of birth. Field observations in the Qinling Mountains recorded most matings in March and April; pregnancy lasted four to five months overall, including about one and a half to two months after implantation. The same study recorded births from mid-August to early September. Captive records put newborns at about 90 to 130 grams: pink, nearly hairless and blind, they are tiny beside their mother. She nurses the helpless cub in a sheltered den. Zoo observations report that cubs open their eyes at six to eight weeks. In the Qinling field study, young pandas left the den at about three to four months. Litters can include twins. Milk remains important through infancy; captive records show nursing for eight to nine months and social separation may occur later.

Pandas depend on bamboo, whose shoots and leaves change in quality and availability through the year. At Wolong, the preferred bamboo Bashania fangiana mass-flowered and died in 1983, sharply reducing the standing crop. Pandas changed what they ate and, two years later, began using more of a lower-elevation alternative bamboo, Fargesia robusta. In the Qinling Mountains, seasonal shifts between bamboo species were documented among tracked pandas in Foping. A separate Qinling study found seasonal dietary overlap between pandas and wild boar eating shoots, suggesting potential competition for a brief, nutritious food. Connected forest can help pandas reach alternate feeding areas as bamboo resources shift.

Hunting for pelts, farming, timber extraction and settlement reduced the panda’s range and broke mountain forests into isolated patches. China’s fourth national survey, conducted in 2011–2014 and published in 2015, reported 1,864 wild pandas at the end of 2013 and 67 reserves in the range, while noting fragmentation and small populations at risk. A 2021 analysis of those census data found that 25 of 33 populations held about 259 pandas, around 14 percent of the wild total. In 2016 the IUCN changed the species’ Red List category from Endangered to Vulnerable after population growth linked to forest protection and restoration, while recognizing continuing risks. Reserves, forest restoration and corridors aim to reconnect habitat, but isolated groups remain vulnerable to habitat loss and limited exchange.

Golden jackal
Canis aureus
The golden jackal is a medium-sized Eurasian canid: a flexible hunter and scavenger that also eats plant matter.

Adults stand about 44–50 cm at the shoulder, with a head-and-body length of 80–105 cm and a 20–30 cm tail. In Europe, males weigh about 11–16 kg and females about 8–13 kg. The coat ranges from cream-gold to tawny, with dark, mixed hairs along the back, pale throat and underside, and a bushy tail often dark at its tip. Long legs, a pointed muzzle and rounded ears help distinguish it from a fox. A small Gujarat, India sample averaged 8.8 kg for adult males (n=6) and 7.3 kg for females (n=4), illustrating population-specific sex differences.

Across Eurasia the species occupies scrub, grassland, woodland, wetlands, farmland and rural edges. In south-eastern Europe, it often uses lowland marshes or mosaics of small fields and dense scrub: open ground offers food, while thickets provide daytime cover and breeding sites.

The jackal searches for food alone or with its family, seizing small mammals—especially rodents—as well as hares, birds, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates. It also eats fallen fruit and other plant matter, and readily scavenges carcasses, discarded livestock remains and refuse where these are accessible. A review of European studies found that the balance changes with place and season: fruit is more common in summer and autumn, while ungulate remains and domestic-animal foods increase in winter. It combines active hunting of small prey with scavenging, often shifting toward the most accessible local food rather than relying on one prey type.

The usual social unit is a breeding pair with the current litter; one or more older offspring may remain on the territory and help. A camera study of one Greek island family documented a stable adult pair and two yearlings that helped care for six pups, illustrating cooperation without making every group identical. Jackals mark and defend territories, and their complex howls carry between groups; in eastern Bulgaria, responses to broadcast calls peaked in summer, when groups answered together. Activity is chiefly nocturnal or crepuscular, although local disturbance and cover affect when animals emerge. Dispersing young can travel hundreds of kilometres to find a territory and mate.

In Europe, mating generally takes place in winter and births follow about 60–63 days later, usually in spring; timing shifts with latitude and local conditions. Litters commonly contain four or five pups, although larger litters have been recorded. European field accounts estimate that pups remain in a den, often an old fox or badger burrow, for about seven weeks. They then follow adults to forage and may return to the den until around fourteen weeks old. Females may mature at 10–11 months, but young adults can delay breeding and help raise a later litter. Both parents provision offspring, and older helpers may assist.

As a mid-sized predator, the jackal takes many rodents and other small prey, while its scavenging removes carcasses and animal waste from some landscapes. The European diet review describes it as a potential consumer of crop pests, especially where rodents are abundant, although the size of this service depends on local food webs and waste practices. A north-eastern Italian study found dietary overlap with red foxes and partial partitioning of prey and habitat: competition is possible, but overlap alone does not establish food limitation. A recent continental model based on European playback surveys identified wolf presence as the strongest predictor limiting jackal occurrence; human presence weakened the modeled relationship, so this association does not by itself demonstrate aggression at encounters.

The IUCN global assessment, published in 2018 and last assessed on 10 January 2018, classifies the golden jackal as Least Concern and records an increasing trend. In Europe, persecution and habitat change contributed to a marked contraction during the first half of the twentieth century. Legal protection in Balkan strongholds helped recovery from the 1950s, followed by natural expansion north and west. A 2023 European monitoring synthesis estimated presence across about 765,000 km² and reported expansion in 21 countries, while warning that reliable population totals are unavailable. France’s first confirmed record was in Haute-Savoie in 2017. The OFB’s March 2026 map documents scattered detections through 2025, with no confirmed reproduction in the country. Across Eurasia, local declines remain associated with habitat conversion, persecution or hunting, while the IUCN notes sparse data in parts of Asia.
