House mouse
Mus musculus

The house mouse, Mus musculus, is a small rodent whose global spread followed human food storage and transport. Its ancestral range lay in Asia, and it now occurs on most continents and many islands. Some populations live in buildings and farms; others forage outdoors. A flexible diet and rapid breeding when conditions permit help it exploit varied settings. But populations differ: mice in food-rich buildings often remain close to nests, while outdoor populations tend to disperse farther. On islands where people introduced them, they can become damaging invaders.

An adult measures about 65–95 millimetres from nose to rump; its tail is usually nearly as long, and mass is about 12–30 grams. Large rounded ears, dark eyes and a nearly bare tail marked by rings of scales help identify it; its proportions and tail distinguish it from short-tailed voles. Fine whiskers read air currents and nearby surfaces. Incisors grow continuously: hard enamel coats the front, while softer dentine behind wears faster, preserving a sharp cutting bevel. Molars grind food.

The species occupies buildings, barns, granaries, cultivated fields, hedgerows and wooded margins. A mouse may spend summer in a field and move into a barn or house as autumn cools. Inside, cracks, wall cavities, stored goods and debris offer shelter beside food; outside, burrows and rock crevices conceal nests. They line nests with shredded fibres. Human settlements let them persist in places too cold or dry for independent survival. Ships and later cargo carried populations to remote islands.

The mouse is an opportunistic omnivore. Wild foods include seeds, grains, green plants, roots and insects; near people it takes stored food and scraps. Switching among foods helps it persist when one resource dwindles. Mice feed in frequent small bouts: UC Agriculture and Natural Resources reports up to one fifth of body mass per day and roughly 200 small meals nightly. Moist foods supply water, but dry diets and heat increase drinking.

Mice are often active at night. Smell, hearing and whiskers help them navigate; scent cues signal social and reproductive information, and males can produce ultrasonic courtship songs. Social structure changes with density and setting. In commensal colonies, a dominant male may defend a territory containing females and young; family members repel outsiders. In wild populations, territories are less distinct and ranges may overlap. A long-term study of free-living mice in a Swiss barn found patterned social contacts, while also showing how ordinary movement could generate some apparent group structure. Young males often leave after conflict; females more often remain nearby.

Where food and shelter remain available, mice can breed throughout the year; outdoor breeding is often seasonal. Pregnancy lasts about 19–21 days, and a litter usually has five or six pups. Newborns are blind and hairless; fur grows by about day ten, eyes open near two weeks, and weaning occurs around three weeks. Young become sexually mature at about five to seven weeks, although wild populations vary with season and conditions. In some wild populations, females share nests and nurse pups communally. Young females are more likely than males to remain near their mother\'s territory; adult aggression often drives young males away.

Mice eat seeds and invertebrates and are prey for owls, hawks, snakes, foxes, weasels and cats. At high density they can consume grain that would otherwise feed other animals. On some remote islands, introduced mice also attack seabird eggs and chicks. In 2021 on Gough Island, researchers found wounded breeding Tristan Albatrosses; one female was later found dead beside her nest after a mouse-inflicted wound. In 2023 on Marion Island, two wounded adult Wandering Albatrosses and eight carcasses were found. The cause of those Marion deaths remained undetermined, although two fresh carcasses bore wounds consistent with mouse attacks. Such effects are local, not typical of every population.

The Mammal Diversity Database, consulted in October 2026, reports the IUCN global category as Least Concern, consistent with the species’ broad distribution. That global category does not describe every local impact. Introduced mice can threaten native wildlife on islands. Around people, control addresses food contamination, property damage and pathogens; rodenticides can also harm non-target animals. Management priorities therefore vary: the species remains globally widespread, while some island ecosystems face pressure from introduced populations.

Humpback whale
Megaptera novaeangliae

The humpback whale is a baleen whale found in all major oceans. Most populations migrate between high-latitude feeding grounds and warmer breeding areas, but the Arabian Sea population remains in its region year-round. Males sing patterned songs, and South Pacific research documents song themes spreading socially between populations.

Adults have a stocky dark-grey body, a broad flattened head and a small dorsal fin behind the midpoint; the fin varies in shape. Females average about 15 metres and are slightly longer than males in NOAA’s Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory account. The pectoral fins reach roughly one-third of body length; fleshy tubercles on the head and lower jaw bear sensory hairs. Researchers identify individuals by the distinctive black-and-white pattern beneath each broad fluke.

Migratory populations typically feed in cold, productive high-latitude waters in summer and move to tropical or subtropical breeding grounds in winter. Some whales travel up to 8,000 kilometres between feeding and breeding grounds; routes differ among populations and hemispheres. Southern populations commonly breed from July to October and feed near Antarctica from November to March; northern populations follow the opposite seasonal cycle. Arabian Sea whales are resident rather than migratory, using warm regional waters that also provide feeding opportunities through seasonal upwelling.

Prey varies geographically: Southern Hemisphere whales mainly take Antarctic krill, while northern populations eat small schooling fish including herring, anchovies and sand lance. During a lunge, a whale engulfs prey-rich water; expandable throat grooves let the mouth and ventral pouch distend. It then expels water through fringed baleen plates that retain prey. In Southeast Alaska, solitary tagged whales formed bubble curtains around krill layers before lunging through the concentrated prey. This detailed bubble-net mechanism is documented at that Alaskan feeding site and does not establish a universal tactic.

Breeding groups are fluid: a female may travel with a calf and a principal male escort, while other males join and jostle for close position. Off eastern Australia, observed males used both escorting and singing tactics; whether song attracts females or mediates competition remains debated. In Hawaiian breeding-area recordings, social “wops” and “grumbles” varied with group context and were quieter when a nearby singing whale could hear them. South Pacific recordings show song themes spreading between populations and some singers combining old and newly introduced material during rapid song change.

Mating and birth occur mainly in warm lower-latitude waters during each hemisphere’s winter; gestation lasts about 11 to 11.5 months. A pregnant female feeds on temperate or polar grounds to build reserves before returning to give birth; she may reach breeding areas before other whales. Females usually have one calf every two or three years, and mother-calf pairs often use shallow, sheltered water. Calves nurse for about 10 to 11 months; compiled estimates place their length near 4.3 metres at birth and 8.8 metres at weaning. In Exmouth Gulf, resting lactating females had respiration rates about half those of adults on feeding grounds, consistent with rest conserving maternal energy.

Baleen whales release nitrogen, phosphorus and iron near the surface in waste, and these nutrients can support phytoplankton growth. A recent model including humpbacks among several whale species estimated variable regional and seasonal effects of whale nutrient recycling on primary production. The model does not isolate a global contribution attributable to humpbacks alone.

NOAA reports that commercial whaling greatly reduced all humpback populations and depleted most by more than 95 percent before the commercial-whaling moratorium. An IWC assessment found strong overall North Pacific recovery from the low level around 1966, with a peak in 2014 and regional declines linked to the 2014–2016 marine heatwave. The CSG’s 2025-2 summary lists the species globally as Least Concern but the Arabian Sea and Oceania subpopulations as Endangered. The global Least Concern assessment was published in November 2018; the separate Arabian Sea assessment is dated 2008. Current pressures include entanglement in fishing gear and debris, vessel strikes and disturbance, underwater noise, and climate-related changes to prey; their effects vary by region. NOAA notes that entanglement can impair feeding or cause injury and death, while prey shifts may worsen nutritional condition and affect reproduction.

European Storm Petrel
Hydrobates pelagicus

The European storm petrel is one of the smallest seabirds of the North Atlantic. It spends nearly its whole life over the open ocean and comes ashore only in summer, at night, to nest on remote islands.

A bird barely larger than a house martin, about 14–18 cm long with a wingspan of 36–39 cm; adults weigh around 26 g. The plumage is dark brownish-black with a broad white patch on the rump and a pale band under each wing. The tail is short and square-ended, unlike the forked tail of Leach’s petrel, and the small bill has a tube on top.

It lives almost entirely at sea. In summer it breeds on remote, small, rat-free offshore islands and a few isolated headlands on the Atlantic fringe of north and west Britain and Ireland. Outside the breeding season it is best seen from headlands in autumn, when onshore winds bring birds closer to land.

It picks small fish, crustaceans and plankton from the sea surface. It feeds by fluttering low over the waves with its wings held in a V, its webbed feet pattering on the water so that it seems to run across it. A good sense of smell helps it find food over open ocean.

It visits its colonies only at night and nests underground, and it often stays at sea on bright moonlit nights, which makes it hard to see in the breeding season. From its burrow it sings a purring call mixed with grunts and squeaks. At sea it often feeds in flocks and follows ships, especially trawlers.

A pair lays a single egg, incubated by both sexes for 38–50 days. The downy chick stays in the nest for 56–73 days before fledging. There is typically one brood a year, and breeding typically starts at about four years of age. The nest is made among rocks or in a burrow.

The storm petrel feeds on small animals of the surface waters and depends on healthy seas. Colonies are found mainly on islands free of rats and other mammalian predators, which threaten eggs and chicks.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern, and it is Amber-listed in the UK. The UK breeding population was about 26,000 nests in 1998–2002, with an uncertain trend, though some colonies have grown, with a doubling on Mousa. It is long-lived: the oldest ringed bird reached over 38 years.

Idaea flaveolaria

Idaea flaveolaria is a small geometrid moth associated in Europe with alpine habitats. French naturalist records place it in the Alpine massif, where its bright coloration makes it noticeable in sunny mountain meadows. Its caterpillar and feeding ecology are much less well known than its adult appearance and distribution.

The adult is a small moth with vivid yellow-orange to warm-brown wings and fine transverse lines that may be clearer underneath; a dark discal spot can also show below. Lepidoptera Mundi gives a wingspan of about 12–16 mm. The combination of color and markings helps separate it from similar Idaea, but worn specimens and locality still matter.

In France, the species is recorded from the Alpine massif; European records are likewise associated with mountain regions. French observations describe sunny, flower-rich high-altitude meadows. This is a localized alpine distribution, not a general species of lowland gardens or farmland.

The larva is thought to be polyphagous, but its food plants and feeding behavior have not been observed adequately in the field according to the French species account. Adult feeding details are not established in the sources reviewed. The food-plant gap is therefore part of the species’ known natural-history uncertainty.

Adults may be seen flying in sunshine over alpine meadows. The French observatory describes this as a sun-loving, conspicuous small moth. Detailed observations of daily activity, courtship and overwintering stages were not available in the sources used for this profile.

The sources reviewed do not document the egg, larval and pupal schedule of I. flaveolaria in enough detail to describe it confidently. The caterpillar’s natural food plants and habits are explicitly noted as unobserved, so a fuller breeding account would be speculative.

The species is part of the alpine moth community and is linked to sunny meadow habitat. The French observatory considers it rare at the scale of its recording grid and notes that larval ecology remains unresolved. No specific pollination, prey or population effect is quantified by the reviewed sources.

A French moth observatory describes the species as rare on its survey grid and its French distribution as limited to the Alps. That local observation is not a global conservation assessment. No verified global IUCN category or population trend was found for this profile.

Greater one-horned rhinoceros
Rhinoceros unicornis

This Asian herbivore is native to the northern Indian subcontinent. Wild populations persist in scattered sites in India and Nepal, especially river floodplains. Its distribution reflects the link between grazing, abundant grass, water and seasonal wetlands.

Adults bear one dark nasal horn of compacted keratin, not bone. Thick grey-brown skin folds at the neck, shoulder and hindquarters, with raised bumps on the shoulders and upper legs. Its flexible upper lip gathers food; young rhinos develop adult folds as they mature.

It favours low alluvial grasslands beside large rivers, with marshes, reed beds, pools and woodland. Flooding renews the plains, producing patches of tall grass and wet ground. Rhinos bathe and wallow, may move higher as floods rise, and also use dry grassland and forest edges.

Grasses, including tall riverine growth, form most of its diet. It also eats aquatic plants, leaves, shoots, twigs and fruit, varying its menu with season and vegetation. Its flexible upper lip gathers plants; it sometimes feeds partly submerged.

Adults are usually solitary, though females stay with calves and animals may gather at grazing sites or wallows. Males hold loosely defended ranges and mark with dung and urine. Activity often peaks in cooler hours. Bathing and wallowing help with heat and biting insects; rhinos also rub against vegetation.

After about 15–16 months, a female gives birth to one calf. Breeding has no fixed annual season, and births are years apart. The calf soon walks and nurses; weaning takes about 12–18 months. Maternal care continues as it learns to forage and becomes independent.

This large herbivore changes plant cover through grazing, trampling and paths. Dung returns seeds and nutrients to floodplain soil, and other wildlife uses its muddy wallows. These effects vary with local conditions.

The IUCN’s 2019 Red List assessment classified it as Vulnerable, estimating 2,100–2,200 mature animals in 11 subpopulations and noting habitat decline. This dated assessment is not a current census. The International Rhino Foundation later reported about 4,075 wild animals after recovery under protection in India and Nepal. Poaching, floodplain habitat loss and fragmentation, and conflict near crowded reserves remain concerns.

Castor Bean Tick
Ixodes ricinus

The castor bean tick, also called sheep tick, is a blood-feeding hard tick, an arachnid and not an insect, and an important tick of medical and veterinary concern in Europe. It waits on vegetation for passing animals and can carry the agents of Lyme disease and tick-borne encephalitis.

Before feeding, adult males are about 2.5–3 mm long and females 3–4 mm; a fed female can reach about 1 cm and turns light grey. Adults are red-brown and have no eyes. The dorsal shield covers the whole back of the male but only the front part of the female. Larvae have three pairs of legs, while nymphs and adults have four.

It occurs from Portugal to Russia and from North Africa to Scandinavia, mainly in deciduous and mixed forest, and is scarce in hot, dry parts of the Mediterranean. It needs relative humidity of at least 80% and can live in grassland, heathland, parks and conifer woods where hosts are present. Its range has shifted to higher altitudes and latitudes in several countries.

It feeds only on blood. Larvae and nymphs mostly take small or medium animals such as wood mice, birds and reptiles, while adults feed mainly on large mammals like cattle, sheep and deer. All stages will bite humans, and each active stage feeds for several days on a single host.

The tick ambushes hosts by climbing to the tips of vegetation and waiting. Because it loses water while questing, it must go back down to the leaf litter to rehydrate, so its activity follows temperature and humidity. Activity often peaks in spring and again in autumn.

The life cycle has four stages (egg, larva, nymph, adult) and three hosts, taking up to three years in one source and two to four in another. After a blood meal, a female waits 4–8 weeks and lays up to 2,000 eggs, and larvae hatch about eight weeks later. Mating can last up to a week.

It transmits many pathogens, including the Lyme borreliosis bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato, tick-borne encephalitis virus, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Babesia and louping ill virus. Milder winters and warm springs make questing start earlier, and snow cover helps overwintering by keeping the ground above freezing.

The species is not threatened; it is expanding its range in several European countries, and models project establishment across Norway, Finland and Sweden by 2071–2100. It is not found in North America, and no Red List assessment was read.

Jaguar
Panthera onca

The jaguar is the largest cat native to the Americas and the only living member of its genus there. Its range stretches from Mexico through Central America into South America, with its strongest continuous populations centered on the Amazon basin.

A jaguar has a compact, muscular body, broad head, short limbs and a tawny to reddish coat. Dark rosettes usually contain smaller central spots; their arrangement differs across the two flanks. Some individuals are melanistic, so rosettes remain faintly visible on black fur.

It favors dense lowland forest, wetlands and river margins, where cover and water are close, but also occupies scrub, savanna and some dry woodland. In the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, it uses wooded and riparian corridors rather than rainforest alone.

This obligate carnivore takes prey ranging from reptiles and fish to large mammals. Peccaries, deer, capybaras, tapirs, caimans and turtles feature in regional diets; livestock may be taken where natural prey has declined. Its strong jaws help dispatch armored reptiles, including by biting through shells.

Jaguars generally live and hunt alone, and scent or scratch marks help signal territorial use. Activity is mainly nocturnal, though individuals may move at any hour as conditions change. Hunting relies on concealment, a short rush and a forceful pounce rather than prolonged pursuit.

Breeding can occur throughout the year across much of the range, although seasonality appears at its northern and southern edges. After roughly 100 days of gestation, a female gives birth to one to four cubs, usually two, in a sheltered den and raises them alone.

As a large predator, the jaguar consumes many animals and can influence prey populations in the ecosystems it occupies. It also depends on connected territories, freshwater and adequate prey. Forest fragmentation can therefore disrupt both its movements and access to food or mates.

Habitat conversion and fragmentation, prey depletion, illegal trade and retaliatory killing all pressure jaguar populations. Livestock losses can bring conflict where ranches overlap with jaguar habitat. Protecting connected landscapes, wild prey and practical coexistence measures addresses several linked pressures across the species’ range.

Eurasian Wryneck
Jynx torquilla
The Eurasian wryneck is an unusual woodpecker that rarely climbs trees. It is named for its snake-like way of twisting its head, and it is the only European woodpecker to migrate over long distances.

A slim bird 16–18 cm long, weighing about 33 g, with a wing near 90 mm. The plumage is delicately patterned in grey, brown and buff, with a dark band running from the nape onto the back and arrowhead-shaped marks on the creamy underparts. The bill is short and less dagger-like than other woodpeckers’.

It is mainly a bird of grassland and open country. In Britain it was once found on commons, heathland, orchards, parkland and larger gardens of central and southern England, and it nests in existing holes, wall crevices, banks or nest boxes.

It eats almost entirely ants, which it collects on the ground, along with beetles and their larvae, moths, spiders and woodlice. It catches prey with its tongue and forages mostly by hopping on the ground with the tail raised.

Unlike other woodpeckers it seldom climbs trunks. It can turn its head nearly 180 degrees, and when disturbed at the nest its neck twists in all directions while it hisses; this snake-like display is thought to deter predators. It sometimes feigns death.

It uses no nesting material. A clutch is typically 7–10 eggs (observed 5–12), incubated for 12–14 days, mainly by the female. The naked, helpless chicks fledge after 18–22 days, and there is usually one brood. Breeding typically starts at one year of age.

The wryneck depends on ant supplies and on ready-made cavities and crevices, as it builds no nest of its own. It migrates to tropical Africa and to southern Asia from Iran to the Indian subcontinent, and passes through Britain in spring and autumn.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern; the world population is estimated at up to 15 million and may be declining slightly. In Britain it has been lost as a breeder: the last confirmed breeding record was in 2002, and it is now a scarce passage migrant, mostly seen in August and September.

Common kingfisher
Alcedo atthis

The Common kingfisher is a small hunter of waterways, often watching fish from a low branch before plunging into the water. It ranges across Europe, North Africa and much of Asia. A European synthesis of ringing records found movement most marked in northern populations, while most adults and juveniles were sedentary; winter dispersal varies by region and age. Its piping call can reveal the bird before its bright colours do.

Adults are typically 16–17 cm long. The compact body carries a long dark bill, blue-green upperparts and orange underparts. The blue is structural: a spongy keratin-and-air layer in the feather barbs, branches along its shaft, coherently scatters light, rather than relying on blue pigment. Both sexes look alike at a distance, but the female’s lower bill is orange-red with a dark tip, whereas the male’s bill is almost entirely black. British ringing samples average 39 g for adults and 36 g for juveniles.

It uses slow rivers, streams, canals, lakes and marshes where fish can be watched from a perch and caught in shallow water. Clear water can make prey easier to see, but field studies also find kingfishers in small wetlands and ponds away from the nest, so a riverbank alone does not define its feeding habitat. Open, steep earth or sand banks provide places to excavate a nesting tunnel. Bank reinforcement, channel straightening and intensive river works remove nesting faces and can sever feeding reaches and habitat corridors.

Small fish make up most of the diet, although aquatic insect larvae and crustaceans are also taken. It watches from a perch, then dives after a fish; surface refraction shifts the prey’s apparent position. Experiments with this species found more attacks and higher capture success in shallow tanks, consistent with prey being more accessible there. After a catch, it beats the fish against its perch to stun it, swallows it head-first, and later regurgitates indigestible bones in a pellet. A study on Italy’s River Ticino found fish in pellets collected at resting sites from March to October 2019, documenting diet outside nesting but not in winter.

Outside courtship and nesting, adults usually forage alone and defend stretches of water that supply dependable fish and perches. A rival may be chased or confronted in a prolonged display, and fights can become physical. Courtship includes the male presenting fish to the female, linking food delivery with pair formation.

The pair excavates a tunnel in an earth or sand bank, usually ending in a bare chamber. In Britain, five to seven eggs are typical. Both adults incubate for about 20 days, and the naked, dependent chicks remain in the nest for roughly 23–26 days. Hampshire nest observations found that fish delivered grew larger as nestlings developed. In observations from Chiplun, Maharashtra, both parents fed chicks, and fledglings continued begging near the nest for about a week. In Britain, one or two broods are usual and three are recorded in favourable seasons.

The kingfisher catches small fish and aquatic invertebrates, while its eggs and nestlings can be preyed upon by snakes and other ground-dwelling animals. In the River Ticino, pellet analysis found mainly common native fish and fewer introduced fish than expected from their availability, showing how this local predator selects prey.

Cold snaps can freeze fishing waters and cause heavy mortality. Pollution, sediment and river engineering can reduce prey visibility or remove nesting banks. North Rhine-Westphalia’s state nature conservation agency identifies bank reinforcement, channel modification, contaminated runoff and disturbance at nest sites as local pressures. BirdLife’s 2024 global IUCN record classifies the species as Least Concern. In the 2021 European assessment, published by the EU in 2022, it is also Least Concern, though the trend remains downward at a slower rate than in 2015, when it was Vulnerable. These dated assessments use different geographic scales and do not establish that every regional population is secure.

Koala
Phascolarctos cinereus

The koala is an Australian marsupial whose range follows eucalypt forests and woodlands across Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and a small part of South Australia. Its distribution is broad but patchy: suitable food trees, soils and local conditions determine where animals can persist. It is the sole living member of the family Phascolarctidae and spends most of its life in trees.

Adults have a large rounded head, conspicuous furry ears, a broad black nose and dense grey to brown fur, usually paler on the chest, inner limbs and rump. Their strong limbs and curved claws grip trunks; two opposable digits on each forepaw help secure a hold while climbing. Males tend to be larger and have a prominent chest scent gland, while females have a pouch opening towards the rear. Size and coat thickness vary geographically, with northern animals generally smaller and lighter than southern ones.

Koalas occupy open forests and woodlands from tropical Queensland to temperate southern Australia, including some fragmented and urban landscapes. Habitat quality depends especially on the local mixture and abundance of food trees; fertile soils and watercourses often support higher densities. Koalas also use non-food trees for resting and shelter, including during extreme weather. Because preferred tree species differ by region and season, suitable habitat is a network of feeding and refuge trees rather than simply any stand of eucalypts.

Leaves of selected Eucalyptus, Corymbia and related trees make up almost all the diet; a koala may eat roughly half a kilogram of foliage daily, although intake varies. It does not choose every tree of a favoured species: leaf water and nutrients matter, as do defensive chemicals such as terpenes and phenolic compounds. The koala’s ridged molars crush leaves, and its liver processes some absorbed toxins. In the hindgut, an enlarged caecum and proximal colon retain fluids, microbes and fine particles for extended fermentation, while less digestible coarse material passes more quickly. This slow, selective processing extracts nutrients from fibrous leaves but yields little energy, so activity is economical and rest is prolonged. Free-ranging females have been observed increasing foliage intake during peak lactation, with digestive adjustments that preserve nutrient extraction.

Koalas are mainly solitary, but neighbouring home ranges often overlap and allow encounters. They rest for much of the day, commonly wedged in a tree fork, and feed or move more often at night and around dawn and dusk. Ground travel between trees exposes them to danger, so connected tree cover matters. Males advertise during the breeding season with deep bellows and scent marks from the chest gland; interactions and movement increase as animals seek mates or compete. These signals help coordinate contact across a dispersed population rather than forming stable social groups.

After a gestation of about 35 days, a female usually gives birth to one very small, hairless joey. It crawls unaided to the rear-opening pouch and attaches to a teat, where it continues developing for around six months. At first emergence it begins tasting the mother’s soft faecal pap, which transfers maternal gut microbes that contribute to foliage digestion. The young then rides on her back and continues nursing while learning to feed; weaning is usually complete near its first birthday. It may remain within its mother’s range before dispersing, often around two to three years old. Timing of births and breeding varies with region and conditions.

The koala’s close dependence on a short list of tree species ties its distribution to the composition and condition of forest. It uses several tree types for shelter as well as food, and moves among them to forage, rest and meet other koalas. Fragmentation can therefore separate feeding patches and make ground crossings more frequent. Drought, heat and fire can reduce foliage quality or availability, while disease, dogs and vehicles add direct mortality; effects differ among regions and populations.

The koala’s conservation situation varies geographically. Under Australia’s EPBC Act, the combined populations of Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory were listed as Endangered on 12 February 2022. Queensland also changed its state category to Endangered on 8 April 2022, and New South Wales did so on 20 May 2022. The 2022 national recovery plan reports the whole species as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, while Victoria and South Australia are outside that federal endangered listing. Habitat loss and fragmentation, climate-related heat and drought, disease, vehicle strikes and dog attacks are interacting pressures. The recovery plan therefore prioritizes connected habitat and coordinated action across jurisdictions; local population trends and legal categories should not be generalized to the entire range.

Laetacara curviceps

Laetacara curviceps is a small cichlid from the lower Amazon basin in Brazil. It inhabits tributaries and quiet waters and is often called the flag acara or smiling dwarf cichlid. The curved head profile behind its scientific name and the dark markings on the body help distinguish it, but identification among Laetacara requires attention to fin markings and close relatives.

It is a compact, deep-bodied fish with a rounded head and dark markings, including a spot near the base of the dorsal fin in many individuals. FishBase lists maximum records of 4.6 cm standard length for male or unsexed fish and 6.6 cm total length for a female; these use different measurement conventions and are not directly comparable. The dorsal-fin spot is shared with close relatives; compared with L. dorsigera, diagnostic details include a deeper head and the absence of the bright red belly shown by breeding L. dorsigera. Color can vary with sex and breeding condition.

Records place the species in lower tributaries of the Amazon in Brazil, including the central lower-Amazon region. It is associated with shallow, slow-moving water and vegetated margins. FishBase records a tropical freshwater, benthopelagic fish; aquarium sources describe soft to moderately hard water but those husbandry parameters should not be mistaken for a complete measurement of wild conditions.

The species is described as a small-prey forager, taking aquatic invertebrates such as insect larvae, small crustaceans and other zooplankton; algae and organic detritus may also be taken. The field diet is not quantified in the accounts used here. Aquarium sources recommend varied small foods, but those recommendations are husbandry guidance rather than evidence of the exact natural diet.

Outside breeding, it is considered relatively peaceful for a cichlid. Pairs defend a small area when spawning, and the species is reported to forage near the bottom and among cover. Aquarium observations are useful for suggesting behavior but do not establish how every wild population behaves.

Laetacara curviceps is a biparental substrate spawner: both parents tend and guard eggs and young. FishBase reports a clutch around 300 eggs, while other accounts describe eggs deposited on a cleaned surface and parental care of larvae. Exact clutch size and timing can vary and are not treated here as fixed species-wide values.

By feeding on small aquatic animals and using shallow vegetated habitats, it links invertebrate prey with larger predators in Amazonian streams. The reviewed sources do not quantify its population role or interactions in the wild. It is also traded for aquaria, but trade is not evidence on its abundance or conservation status.

FishBase reports a global IUCN assessment of Least Concern dated 7 November 2018. That is a dated global assessment, not a guarantee that every local population is stable. The sources reviewed here do not provide a more recent population trend or a current reassessment.

Black Garden Ant
Lasius niger

The black garden ant is the familiar small dark ant of lawns, paths and pavements in Europe. Its colonies are led by a queen that is exceptionally long-lived for an insect, with lifespans of 20 years and more reported, while workers live for a much shorter and more variable time.
Workers are small, about 3 to 5 mm long, and dark brown to almost black. The winged females seen during swarms are larger, up to about 9 mm, while winged males measure about 3.5 to 4.5 mm.

It is common in built-up areas and often found in drier places. Nests lie in the ground, in lawns, flower pots, compost bins and among plant roots, often under rocks or paving. The main sign of a nest is a small heap of fine soil at the surface.
It eats other invertebrates and collects honeydew, the sugary liquid excreted by aphids and some other sap-feeding insects. Workers can often be seen tending aphids.

Colonies hold many hundreds to thousands of ants, and large nests can pass 20,000. Ants may guard aphids from ladybirds and other predators to protect their honeydew supply. Young queens and males swarm in warm, humid weather, mainly from July to August, and swarms occur over several weeks rather than on a single day.

During the nuptial flight a queen usually mates with several males and stores enough sperm to lay fertilised eggs for the rest of her life. Males live only a day or two afterwards. The queen then chews off her wings, digs an underground chamber, lays her first eggs and raises them without feeding for weeks, until her first workers can forage.

In gardens the ants prey on other invertebrates and, by protecting aphids, can raise plant damage; they do little direct harm to plants. Their excavated soil can bury low plants and disturb the roots of potted plants. The Royal Horticultural Society advises tolerating them as part of garden biodiversity.
No global conservation assessment was found. The species is common and widespread in gardens and built-up areas of Europe, and no threat has been identified in the sources consulted.

West Indian Ocean Coelacanth
Latimeria chalumnae

The West Indian Ocean coelacanth is a large, deep-water fish of the western Indian Ocean. Its paired fins sit on fleshy lobes and move in a diagonal pattern, like the legs of a four-limbed land animal. The best-known population lives around the Comoro Islands.

The body is dark metallic blue with irregular white or pale bluish spots, a pattern unique to each fish, and it turns brownish after death. The head is naked, the lower jaw has two large overlapping plates, and the brain fills only about 1% of the cranial cavity. Females are larger, reaching about 2 m, while males stay around 1.7 m.

It lives on steep rocky slopes at 150–700 m, usually 180–250 m, in water of 13–25 °C, and shelters in caves by day. Besides Grande Comore and Anjouan in the Comoros, populations are known from South Africa, Madagascar and Mozambique.

It preys on fishes and squid, and known prey includes Beryx fishes, cardinalfishes, a skate, an eel and a swell shark. It does not chase prey but snaps up animals that pass within about 20 cm of its mouth.

It is nocturnal. By day several fish gather in caves, though no social interaction has been seen; at night each drifts alone in search of food, covering several kilometres. Tagged fish travelled 2–8 km in a day, and the species can swim in any direction, even upside down.

It is ovoviviparous: the eggs, about 9 cm across, develop inside the female, who gives birth to fully formed young of 35–38 cm. Litters of 5 to 29 young have been reported. Gestation is estimated at 13 months or about three years, so females may breed only every second or third year; males give no known care.
The coelacanth is a predator high in the food web, with a trophic level of about 4.4. Humans are its only known predator, and its spotted pattern may help it blend into cave walls.

The IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered (assessed 2000, as reported by FishBase), and international trade is banned under CITES Appendix I. It is not eaten but is caught by accident, mainly in gill nets and deep-water fishing for other species, and the population is believed to be small and declining.

Least weasel
Mustela nivalis

The least weasel has a very slender, elongated trunk, short limbs and a short tail, a form that lets it follow rodents into narrow burrows. Its high surface-to-volume ratio and inability to curl into a compact ball increase heat loss. Its native range spans much of Europe, northern Asia and northern North America, with introductions to some islands.

In Britain, adult males usually measure 19.4–21.7 cm in body length, with a 4.2–5.2 cm tail, and weigh 106–131 g; females measure 17.3–18.3 cm, with a 3.4–4.3 cm tail, and weigh 55–69 g. Adult body size also varies geographically. The British coat is reddish brown above and cream below, with an irregular boundary; its short tail lacks the stoat’s black tip. Some northern populations turn white in winter, unlike Britain’s. In northeastern Poland, observations from 1997 and 2003–07 associated fewer snow-cover days with a smaller share of white winter coats. In a separate 2015–16 experiment, predators detected coat models more often when their colour mismatched the background; snow-cover percentage did not significantly predict detection.

Across its Holarctic range, it uses grassland, meadows, farmland, woodland edges, scrub, steppe, wetlands and some alpine or coastal habitats. It favors ground cover and prey-rich patches for ambushes, and shelters in abandoned rodent nests or burrows, often using several resting sites rather than digging a den.

In a Polish forest, five radio-tracked males attacked bank voles and yellow-necked mice above and below ground. Of 60 observed attacks, success was 23% on voles and 60% on mice, so tunnel access did not guarantee a catch. On English farmland, voles made up 16% of the diet in low-vole years and 54% at peak abundance, while birds became the main alternative when voles were scarce. Smaller weasels consumed more food relative to body mass; captive trials also found assimilation varied with diet and temperature, so they do not define a wild daily ration.

An English woodland study found resident male ranges varied in size and shifted with prey distribution; males generally ranged farther than females. Usually solitary, least weasels mark den sites with scent. Their small bodies need frequent feeding, and surplus prey may be cached near shelters. Measurements of free-ranging males in Poland found higher thermoregulatory costs in cold weather and daily activity adjusted with temperature, body mass, habitat and season.

From 18 breeding females and three immature young sampled in Poland, the author inferred a season from April mating to the last young leaving in October, cautioning that the sample was small. Unlike stoats, least weasels do not delay implantation: total gestation lasts about 34–37 days from mating, including roughly 25 days after implantation. A five-year captive study recorded 65 litters, averaging 5.1 kits among 53 litters of known size; this is not a universal wild average. Newborns weigh about 1–1.7 g and are naked, blind and deaf; ears open at 21–28 days and eyes at 26–30 days. The female alone nurses for about 32 days; weaning may continue to 42–56 days. In captivity, young can kill prey at about 47 days; they disperse and become independent at about nine to ten weeks.

On 25 km² of southern English farmland, vole density peaked at fourteen times its low-year level in a four-year cycle; weasel numbers lagged and females failed to breed in the trough, documenting a local predator response without showing that weasels caused the vole cycle. In Białowieża Forest, winter estimates attributed 11–21% of rodent predation to weasels, compared with 56–71% to tawny owls and 10–15% to pine martens.

The global IUCN assessment dated 2 May 2015 and amended in 2019 lists the species as Least Concern, citing its broad range, presumed large population and tolerance of some habitat change. In Britain, gamekeepers historically trapped weasels as supposed gamebird enemies; the Mammal Society says they probably killed few chicks and that trapping likely had no long-term effect because populations recover and recolonise.

Leopard
Panthera pardus

The leopard is a powerful cat native to Africa and Asia. It occupies a broad range of environments, from tropical forest to desert and mountains. Its flexible hunting and climbing abilities help it persist where other large cats may not.

Adults have a long body, short muscular legs, broad paws and a long tail. Their coats range from pale gold to ochre, with dark rosettes and smaller solid spots. Some are melanistic; their markings remain visible in suitable light.

Leopards use rainforest, woodland, savanna, scrub, rocky slopes and desert where cover and prey are available. They also occur in some human-used landscapes. Himalayan records reach about 5,200 metres, an exceptional local record rather than a typical habitat.

This carnivore hunts prey from small mammals and birds to larger ungulates. Its menu depends on locally available animals: a Gabon study found forest ungulates important, while research in Tanzania recorded substantial primate consumption. Leopards may also take livestock near farms.

Leopards generally live alone, except when females travel with cubs or adults meet to mate. Activity varies: many studied savanna populations are mainly nocturnal, while some in Gabonese rainforest were largely active by day. Scent marks, calls and scratches signal presence.

After about three months of pregnancy, a female gives birth in a concealed den, commonly to two or three cubs. They remain hidden, then follow her and learn to hunt. Independence is gradual; reported ages vary among populations, from about one year to two years.

The leopard consumes different prey in different habitats, so no single species defines its diet everywhere. It may carry a kill into a tree, making it less accessible to competitors. When wild prey is scarce, livestock may enter its diet and cause conflict with people.

The IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group’s account, citing Red List version 2024-2, classifies leopards as Vulnerable and reports an 11% contraction of extant range during 2016–2023. It identifies habitat loss, prey depletion, illegal killing and trade, retaliation, and poorly managed trophy hunting as pressures.

Leopardus braccatus

The Pantanal cat, also called the Brazilian pampas cat or savanna pampas cat, is a small South American wild cat of open country. It was long treated as part of the widespread pampas cat, but a 2020 revision split that group into five species, and this is one of them. Much of what is known comes from the group as a whole.

A study cited by a wild cat conservation group gives averages of about 68 cm head and body, a tail of about 26 cm and a weight near 3.9 kg. Pampas cats in general look like a stocky house cat with a broad face and long hair, sometimes with a crest along the back; their coats range from yellow-white to grey-brown, plain or patterned, and melanistic forms occur.

It lives mainly in Brazil, with records in Paraguay, eastern Bolivia and Argentina, in open areas such as the Cerrado, the Pantanal, the savannas of Beni and the Chiquitano dry forest. The exact limits of its range are still uncertain, because older records were attributed to the broader pampas cat.
No study specific to this species was found. Pampas cats as a group eat mainly small mammals such as rodents and hares, along with birds and occasionally lizards, and hunt mostly on the ground.

Pampas cats are solitary and terrestrial, active at any hour but tending to be more nocturnal. For the Pantanal cat itself, home ranges of about 19.5 to 27.7 square kilometres have been reported in Brazil.

Almost nothing is known about breeding in the wild. Records from captive pampas cats suggest a gestation of 80–85 days and litters of one to three kittens, and these figures may not apply to this species in particular.

As a small ground predator of rodents and birds, it takes a place among the smaller carnivores of open Neotropical habitats. In central Brazil, pampas cats are reported to hybridise with the northern tiger cat, though this record concerns the group as a whole.

The Mammal Diversity Database notes that the species has not been evaluated on the IUCN Red List. A wild cat conservation group describes it as decreasing and Vulnerable, without giving the assessment behind this. Threats named for the group include habitat loss to cropland, livestock and oil extraction, retaliation for poultry losses, road deaths and dog attacks.

Colorado Potato Beetle
Leptinotarsa decemlineata

The Colorado potato beetle is a leaf beetle from North America that became one of the world’s most serious potato pests. It first fed on wild nightshades, moved onto cultivated potato in the 19th century, and later spread across Europe and Asia.

Adults are oval, dome-shaped and 8–10 mm long. Each wing cover bears five black stripes on a yellow ground, and the orange thorax carries black spots. Larvae are soft, plump and hump-backed, with a row of black spots along each side; the eggs are yellow-orange and about 1.7–1.8 mm long.

It lives mostly in fields of potato and other nightshade crops such as tomato, eggplant and pepper, and on wild nightshades in grassland and suburbs. The species originated in the south-western United States and Mexico, spread east of the Rockies, and is now established across Europe, Asia Minor, Iran, Central Asia and China.

Adults and larvae both eat leaves, mainly of Solanum plants. Cultivated potato is the favourite host, ahead of eggplant, tomato, pepper and wild nightshades. A heavy attack can strip a plant down to stems.

Adults and larvae are active by day and inactive at night. Adults can fly several kilometres, especially when crowded, and males release a pheromone that attracts both sexes. Larvae defend themselves by walking away, regurgitating and wiggling.

Adults overwinter in the soil, usually at field edges, and emerge in spring. Females lay clusters of yellow-orange eggs under leaves, up to about 800 in a lifetime. The larvae pass through four stages, then pupate in the soil, and a life cycle lasts about 30 days depending on temperature. There are two or three generations a year, and some adults stay in the soil for more than one winter.

Fungi, predatory insects, toads and birds attack the beetle, but they rarely control it alone. Its resistance to insecticides is a major issue: more than 300 cases have been documented in Asia, Europe and North America.

The species is not threatened; Animal Diversity Web lists its IUCN status as Not Evaluated. It is better known as an agricultural pest, and Great Britain fought three invasions in 1876, 1901 and 1914 with chemical control.

Atlantic Horseshoe Crab
Limulus polyphemus

The Atlantic horseshoe crab is a marine arthropod of the North American coast. Despite its name it is not a crab: it belongs to a separate group, more closely related to arachnids, and is one of four living horseshoe crab species, a lineage with fossil relatives about 450 million years old.

It carries chelicerae, small pincer-like appendages that pass food toward the mouth, and six flap-like abdominal appendages; the first covers the genital pore and the others act as gills. Mature males have claspers used to hold a female, and females may show scars from being clasped.

It lives along the Atlantic coast of North America and the Gulf of Mexico, from Maine to Alabama, with a separate population on the Yucatán Peninsula. It uses shallow coastal water over sandy or muddy bottoms, and tolerates a wide range of environmental conditions.
It feeds at night on worms, small molluscs and algae. It picks food up with its chelicerae, passes it to the bristly leg bases to be crushed, then moves it to the mouth.

It walks along the bottom of shallow water and can swim clumsily on its back, using its flap-like gills as paddles. Individuals are highly mobile and migratory; tagging in Delaware Bay found animals ranging from the bay’s mouth south to Virginia Beach.

Spawning takes place on beaches, where mature males come ashore alone or clasping a female. In a New Hampshire estuary, males appeared to mature at about nine years, after roughly 17 moults, while females moulted once more; this skews spawning-beach sex ratios toward males. Stranding during spawning is a main natural cause of adult death.

In Delaware Bay, the abundance of horseshoe crab eggs was the strongest predictor of which beaches migrating red knots used in spring. The knots, shorebirds on a long migration, have few alternative foods there, so the crab’s spawning supports a wider food web.

The IUCN ranks the species as Vulnerable, and a regional assessment found it vulnerable to local extinction, with risk varying by region: highest in the Gulf of Maine, declines in New England, stable and regulated stocks in Delaware Bay. Bait use removes up to about one million animals a year along the coast. Blood is also taken for Limulus amebocyte lysate, which detects bacterial endotoxin in medicines; about 525,000 crabs were bled yearly in 2013–2017, with short-term mortality estimated at 15%.

The lingcod is a large northeastern Pacific predator in the greenling family Hexagrammidae, not the cod family Gadidae. It ranges from the Gulf of Alaska to Baja California and may live for more than twenty years.

Its elongated body tapers toward the tail and is mottled grey, brown, green or blue, often with copper spots. A broad, unscaled head and large mouth hold many sharp teeth. Canadian records place maturity near 45 centimetres in males and 61–75 centimetres in females. Some have blue-green flesh that loses colour when cooked; its cause remains unknown.

Adults occupy coastal rocky reefs and other complex bottom habitats, with crevices that provide shelter. Adhesive eggs stay in shallow crevices, and larvae drift near the surface. Juveniles settle on nearshore sand among eelgrass or kelp, then move toward deeper reefs as they grow.

Adults seize prey with a sudden lunge, eating bottom fish—including smaller lingcod—as well as octopuses, squid and crabs. Larvae feed on drifting zooplankton such as krill and tiny crustaceans; juveniles switch to small fish.
Lingcod remain near familiar reefs; males defend nesting territories in late autumn while females visit spawning grounds seasonally. Sharks, marine mammals and larger lingcod prey on them.

Males mature near age two and females near three. In winter and spring, females lay adhesive eggs in rocky crevices; males fertilize and guard them for eight to ten weeks. The eggs hatch into drifting larvae that eat plankton, then settle in coastal nurseries and later feed on fish.
Rockfish, sculpins, greenlings and sea stars consume unguarded eggs. Young lingcod enter coastal food webs after feeding on surface plankton.

Commercial and recreational fisheries target lingcod; bottom trawls can disturb habitat and catch other groundfish. NOAA reports both U.S. Pacific stocks were not overfished in 2021 assessments and were not subject to overfishing in 2024. Seasonal closures and limits protect spawning fish.

Lion
Panthera leo

Wild lions now survive in fragmented parts of sub-Saharan Africa and in one Asian population in western India. They use settings from savanna and scrub to dry woodland, while prey and human pressures vary between regions. In India, lions move through the wider Gir landscape, where protected forest meets farms and settlements.

The lion has a muscular, deep-chested body, a short tawny coat, pale underparts and a long tail tipped with a dark tuft; cubs often have fading spots. Adult males usually grow a mane whose length and shade vary with age and individual; females generally lack one. African reference adults average 180 kilograms and 1.20 metres at the shoulder for males, and 130 kilograms and 1.05 metres for females; individuals vary. Asiatic lions often have shorter manes and a more visible abdominal fold. Retractile claws grip prey; long canines kill and cheek teeth slice meat.

Lions occupy savannas, grasslands, scrub, open woodland and dry forests, provided that cover, prey and relatively undisturbed den sites are available. Gir combines dry deciduous forest, thorn scrub, grassland and river corridors within a cultivated regional landscape. Asiatic lions may rest in dense vegetation by day and range more widely at night, sometimes near farms and settlements. A comparison across ten habitats found that seasonal food scarcity, rather than overall prey abundance alone, was linked to larger home ranges.

Lions are opportunistic carnivores, but medium and large hoofed mammals usually supply most of their food. They stalk close before a short rush, then use jaws and forelimbs to bring prey down. Group hunts may divide roles, but observations show that participation varies and some lions hang back when prey is easier to catch. In Gir, chital, sambar, nilgai and wild pigs are documented prey; livestock made up a larger share of recorded kills in peripheral areas than inside the protected landscape.

In many African populations, a pride is a flexible, fission-fusion group built around related females and their young. Males may hold territory in coalitions, while females often stay in their birth group and young males disperse; local patterns vary. Pride members split into smaller parties and reunite to rest, care for cubs, mate or defend territory. Both sexes roar and growl to communicate. Roars maintain contact with pride members and advertise territorial boundaries; lions can use the number of callers they hear to assess the strength of rivals. At Gir, female groups and male coalitions commonly use separate ranges, meeting mainly to mate or at large kills.

Females breed in different seasons; gestation lasts about 110 days and litters usually contain one to four cubs. A mother gives birth in a secluded thicket, hiding the cubs for their first weeks and returning to nurse them. Cubs eat meat from about three months and are weaned near six months, yet Gir young may depend on the natal group for food until two or three years old. Females may first breed at about three and a half years; males often mate only after securing territory. A takeover by unfamiliar males can put cubs at risk; mothers may hide or defend them, and outcomes vary with age and local conditions.

Food scarcity can enlarge territories and reduce prides: a comparison of ten habitats linked lean-season prey availability with group size and cub survival. Lions consume large herbivores, but also compete with other carnivores over carcasses, scavenging and sometimes losing kills to rivals. In Gir, the balance between wild prey and livestock shifts with season and location, linking prey access to local feeding patterns.

The IUCN global assessment, made on 1 February 2023 and published in 2024, lists lions as Vulnerable and the trend as decreasing. It inferred a 36 percent range reduction over three generations, with habitat loss, prey depletion and conflict-related killing among the pressures. African populations are fragmented; Gujarat’s protection and habitat management have supported a recovery, but India’s lions remain concentrated in one regional population. The government reported 891 Asiatic lions in its 2025 count on 10 August 2026.

Little Auk
Alle alle
The little auk, also called the dovekie, is one of the smallest seabirds in the world. It nests in huge Arctic colonies and spends the rest of the year at sea in the North Atlantic.

A little auk is about the size of a Starling: roughly 19–23 cm long, with a wingspan near 40 cm and a weight around 165 g. It is black above and white below, with a stubby black bill, a short neck and tail, and dark underwings. In flight it shows very fast, whirring wingbeats.

It breeds north of the Arctic Circle among rocky scree slopes, eroded cliffs and boulder piles; Svalbard holds about 90% of the world’s breeding birds. Outside the breeding season it lives at sea, often near oceanic fronts, and in Britain it is a winter visitor in the northern North Sea.

It feeds mainly on small planktonic crustaceans such as copepods, amphipods and krill-like euphausiids, with a few small fish, molluscs and worms. It dives down to about 40 m, propelling itself with its wings.

The little auk is social and colonial, flying low over the sea and resting in groups on the water. After breeding it heads south, and strong northerly gales can drive large numbers past the coast or, occasionally, far inland.

Pairs are monogamous and often return to the same nest site, hidden among rocks. A single egg is laid each year and incubated by both parents for 28–31 days. The downy chick fledges after about 23–30 days and leaves the colony at dusk or night, flying out to sea.

By eating huge numbers of zooplankton the little auk links ocean plankton to the Arctic land. Its eggs and chicks are taken by Arctic foxes and glaucous gulls, and the nitrogen-rich droppings of large colonies favour lichens and other nitrogen-tolerant plants beneath the cliffs.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern, and the European population is estimated at about 80 million individuals. It is on the UK Green list. Past local declines were linked to oil spills and to Arctic foxes introduced for fur farming; polluted northern waters remain a risk.

Common Periwinkle
Littorina littorea

The common periwinkle is a sea snail of European rocky shores and the largest British periwinkle. It grazes on algae, is gathered by hand for food, and has been introduced to the north-west Atlantic, where it became the most abundant large invertebrate grazer of the coast.

The shell is sharply conical with a pointed tip, usually black or dark grey-brown with darker spiral lines and a white central column. It is typically about 3 cm high and reaches 5 cm at most. Young shells with spiral ridges can be confused with Littorina saxatilis.

It occurs on rocky shores from the upper shore into shallow subtidal water, except in the most exposed places, and also on sand or mud in sheltered estuaries. It tolerates brackish water. Its native range runs from northern Spain to the White Sea.
It is a grazer feeding mainly on fine green, brown and red algae such as sea lettuce, Cladophora and Ectocarpus. It occasionally eats small animals and the egg capsules of other snails.

In northern Britain it moves down the shore in autumn and back up in spring, depending on local winter temperatures. It hosts several parasitic flatworms, and parasitism by trematodes may cause sterility.

Sexes are separate and fertilisation is internal. Females release egg capsules of about 1 mm, each with usually two or three eggs, directly into the sea, timed with spring tides; a large female can produce up to about 100,000 eggs a year. The larvae feed in the plankton for several weeks, up to six, and the snails mature at 2 to 3 years and live 5 to 10 years.

It is often the dominant grazing snail on the lower shore, and it accumulates trace elements such as silver, cadmium and lead, so it is a suitable bioindicator of marine contamination. It is prey for crabs, fish and birds. In New England its grazing has strongly changed algal communities.

No global conservation category was found. It is hand-gathered without regulation for food, with commercial value in Scotland and Ireland, where collectors have noted fewer large snails. In North America it was first recorded at Pictou, Nova Scotia, in 1840, and is established from Newfoundland to Virginia.

Lowland paca
Cuniculus paca

The lowland paca is a large, mostly nocturnal rodent of tropical America, from eastern Mexico through Central America and much of South America. It belongs to Cuniculidae, the paca family; the agoutis are separate rodents in genus Dasyprocta, despite the similar common name. Its close relative, the mountain paca, is a distinct species associated with higher Andean forests.

Adults commonly weigh about 6–12 kilograms and measure roughly 60–82 centimetres from head to body; males tend to be a little larger. A compact, nearly tailless body, short sturdy legs, blunt head and long whiskers suit this ground-dwelling animal. Its coarse reddish- to dark-brown back bears several lengthwise rows of pale spots, above a lighter belly. The mountain paca is generally smaller and more thickly furred. The agouti is a separate rodent, not another paca.

In the Lacandon rainforest, pacas also use secondary woodland and riparian cover. It favors stream and river banks, which provide den sites and quick access to water as an escape route. A daytime refuge may be a self-dug burrow or a cavity among roots, rocks or an old burrow; several exits can connect to forest paths. In the Lacandon Forest, used cavities lay under roots or inside fallen logs in riparian or secondary vegetation, generally within 100 metres of water.

Fallen fruit is the main food, supplemented by seeds, tender leaves, stems and roots; the exact menu follows local fruiting seasons. A French Guianan stomach-content comparison found that fruit dominated the paca diet, with more seasonal variation than in smaller terrestrial rodents. In the Lacandon Forest of southern Mexico, cameras confirmed fruit at 31 of 57 monitored feeding sites, with fruits from 20 tree species recorded. Only 40 percent of the tree species eaten were shared between preserved and transformed sites, evidence that local pacas use a flexible menu.

By day the paca rests; around dusk it follows familiar trails to feed. Adults are often encountered alone, though some accounts describe territorial pairs using separate burrows. Alarmed pacas may flee into water, stamp, grind their teeth or give a low rumble. Expanded cheek arches and hollows in the upper jaw form a bony chamber proposed to amplify that call, but this acoustic function remains uncertain.

In tropical populations, breeding may occur throughout the year, while some subtropical populations have a seasonal cycle. After roughly 97–118 days of gestation in the wild, a female usually gives birth to one well-developed young; twins are reported but less typical. The young are well developed at birth: their eyes are open and their movements already coordinated, rather than remaining helpless in a nest. They start sampling solid food at about three weeks and are usually weaned within six to twelve weeks; this early development helps a young paca move to shelter and escape danger.

By feeding on fallen fruit, pacas can disperse seeds and support fruit-tree regeneration. Their abandoned burrows provide shelters that other animals may use. Jaguars, ocelots and other predators hunt pacas, which may compete with agoutis and other forest mammals for fruit.

Globally, IUCN lists the paca as Least Concern. The same system reports a Near Threatened Argentine assessment by SAREM in 2025 and a Vulnerable national assessment published in 2021. The paca is among the most heavily hunted Neotropical mammals for food and sport; researchers warn that modest reproductive output may not offset intense hunting. A slow life history, with first parturition only after several months, makes recovery vulnerable to sustained hunting pressure, even where the species remains widespread overall.

Common Earthworm
Lumbricus terrestris

The common earthworm, also called night crawler in North America, is one of the largest earthworms of Europe. It is an epi-anecic species: it lives in a deep, mostly vertical burrow and comes to the surface to feed. It is hermaphroditic, yet each worm still needs a partner to reproduce.

It measures roughly 9 to 30 cm, and the largest individuals are reported at up to 35 cm when stretched in motion. The back is brownish to purplish red and the underside yellow-orange, and the tail end is flattened and paddle-shaped, which lets the worm grip its burrow walls.

It prefers undisturbed soil and is common in lawns and grassland. Its permanent burrow normally reaches 1 to 2 m deep, though one source gives up to 2.5 m. On a very thin topsoil over an inert subsoil in north-west England, worms built shallow U-shaped burrows only about 0.11 m deep and still formed a breeding population.
It feeds mainly on fallen leaves and other decaying plant material, and takes in soil and plant litter as it digs. It is a detritivore that emerges at night.

It emerges mostly at night and anchors itself in its burrow with its broadened tail. It builds small turret-like mounds, called middens, at the burrow entrance. Its burrowing is flexible: in shallow soil it adapts the shape of the burrow rather than going down into hostile subsoil.

Mating takes place on the surface in wet weather, with two worms lying head to tail, and can last up to four hours. Each worm produces on average about 38 cocoons per year according to one source. Individuals typically mature within a year and may live up to about six years.

By eating and expelling mineral and organic matter, it aerates and turns over the soil. Densities of 20 to 40 worms per square metre are reported in an average British lawn, and up to 70 per square metre elsewhere, giving this species one of the largest animal biomasses per hectare on land.
No global conservation assessment was found. In Britain it is described as common and widespread, though badly under-recorded.
